name: Water
scoreRationale: Water is the benchmark for a benign ingredient; it is only harmful at extreme intakes far beyond anything in a product.
summary: Water is the base of most drinks, lotions, shampoos and cleaners. It dissolves the other ingredients so they can be spread, rinsed or absorbed evenly.

profile.function: Formulators use water as the continuous phase of emulsions, the carrier for water-soluble actives, and the diluent that sets a product's concentration and texture.

reactions.title: Autoionization
reactions.description: A tiny fraction of water molecules transfer a proton to each other, which is why pure water has a pH of 7 and why pH can be measured at all.

reactions.title: Hydrolysis
reactions.description: Water splits esters, salts and proteins in the presence of heat, acids, bases or enzymes, which is why water-based products need preservatives and pH control.

mechanisms.title: Hydration of the skin barrier
mechanisms.description: Water plasticizes the stratum corneum's keratin, making skin more flexible; humectants and occlusives in a formula help keep it there.

mechanisms.title: Osmotic balance
mechanisms.description: Cells regulate volume by moving water across membranes through aquaporin channels in response to salt and sugar gradients.

regulatory.status: Tap water must meet National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for over 90 contaminants.
Bottled water is regulated as a food with a standard of identity and quality.
Listed as Aqua (INCI); cosmetic water is typically purified by deionization or reverse osmosis to remove minerals and microbes.

toxicology.mechanism: Drinking many liters within a few hours can dilute blood sodium (hyponatremia), causing brain swelling. This is extremely rare and unrelated to product use.
toxicology.dosage: There is no meaningful risk from water in foods or personal-care products. Hyponatremia generally requires several liters consumed in a short period, often during endurance events.

profile.sensitization: Not an allergen or irritant. Frequent wet work can dry skin because it strips natural oils, not because water is harmful.

myths.claim: "Aqua" is a cheap filler that dilutes a product.
myths.consensus: Water is the solvent that lets actives dissolve, spread and absorb evenly; most lotions and cleansers could not exist without it.

myths.claim: Alkaline or "structured" water has special health effects.
myths.consensus: Stomach acid neutralizes drinking water's pH within minutes, and claims about restructured water have no support in physical chemistry.

steps: Municipal or well water is filtered to remove particulates.
Reverse osmosis forces water through a membrane that rejects dissolved salts.
Ion-exchange resins swap remaining ions for H+ and OH-, which recombine into water (deionization).
UV light or filtration removes microbes for cosmetic and pharmaceutical grades.

environment.persistence: Not applicable: water is part of the natural hydrologic cycle.
environment.notes: The environmental cost of water in products is mostly the energy used to purify, heat and ship it.

fun.history: Henry Cavendish showed in 1781 that burning hydrogen produces water, and Antoine Lavoisier named hydrogen "water-former" in 1783, ending the idea that water was an element.
uses: Water jets cutting steel and stone
Ice as a building material in the Arctic
fun.occurrence: Covers about 71% of Earth's surface and makes up roughly 60% of the adult human body.

name: Sugar
scoreRationale: Chemically benign, but added sugar is one of the clearest dietary risks: excess intake drives dental caries and contributes to weight gain and type 2 diabetes risk.
summary: Table sugar is a plant-derived disaccharide of glucose and fructose. It is safe in small amounts, but most people eat far more added sugar than health guidelines recommend.

physical.solubility: Very soluble in water (about 2,000 g/L at 25 °C); insoluble in oils
physical.phStability: Hydrolyzes in acid, especially when heated

profile.function: Provides sweetness, bulk and moisture retention, feeds yeast in bread, lowers the freezing point of ice cream, and browns during baking. In scrubs it acts as a dissolvable exfoliant.

reactions.title: Inversion (hydrolysis)
reactions.description: Acid or the enzyme invertase splits sucrose into glucose and fructose, the "invert sugar" used in syrups and made by bees in honey.

reactions.title: Caramelization and Maillard browning
reactions.description: Above about 160 °C sucrose breaks down into hundreds of flavor and color compounds; with proteins it drives Maillard browning in baked goods.

mechanisms.title: Digestion and fructose metabolism
mechanisms.description: Intestinal sucrase splits sucrose; glucose enters the bloodstream directly while fructose is processed mainly by the liver, where large intakes promote fat synthesis.

mechanisms.title: Tooth decay
mechanisms.description: Oral bacteria such as Streptococcus mutans ferment sucrose into lactic acid, dissolving enamel, and build sticky glucan plaque from it.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe; "Added Sugars" must be declared on the Nutrition Facts label.
Recommends free sugars below 10% of daily energy, ideally below 5% (about 25 g for adults).
Limit added sugars to less than 10% of calories from age 2; avoid them entirely before age 2.

toxicology.mechanism: Not toxic in the classical sense. Harm comes from chronic excess: repeated blood-glucose and insulin spikes, liver fat accumulation from fructose, and acid attack on teeth.
toxicology.dosage: A teaspoon in a recipe is trivial; the concern is daily totals. One 12-oz regular soda contains about 39 g of sugar, more than the WHO's ideal daily limit.

profile.sensitization: Not an allergen or skin sensitizer. Sugar scrubs can irritate if rubbed too hard on sensitive or broken skin.

myths.claim: Sugar makes children hyperactive.
myths.consensus: Double-blind trials, summarized in a 1995 JAMA meta-analysis, found no effect of sugar on children's behavior; expectations shape what parents observe.

myths.claim: "Natural" sugars like coconut sugar or raw cane sugar are healthier.
myths.consensus: They are still mostly sucrose and count as added sugar; trace minerals are nutritionally negligible.

synthesis.method: Naturally extracted from sugar cane or sugar beet.
steps: Cane is crushed (or beets are sliced into cossettes and soaked in hot water) to release sugar-rich juice.
The juice is clarified with lime and carbon dioxide, which precipitate impurities as calcium carbonate.
Water is evaporated under vacuum to form a syrup.
Seed crystals grow sucrose crystals, which are separated from molasses in centrifuges and dried.

environment.persistence: Not persistent; rapidly consumed by microbes.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Non-toxic, though large spills can deplete oxygen in waterways as microbes consume it.
environment.notes: Cane cultivation drives land-use change and field burning in some regions.

fun.history: Crystalline sugar was first produced in India around the 5th century CE; the Sanskrit "khanda" gave us the word candy. Andreas Marggraf found sucrose in beets in 1747, launching Europe's beet sugar industry.
uses: A set retarder that slows cement hardening
Traditional wound dressing (sugar paste draws water from bacteria)
fun.occurrence: Found in fruit, maple sap, dates, carrots and the nectar of many flowers.

name: Salt
scoreRationale: Essential in small amounts, but typical diets exceed recommended sodium, which raises blood pressure in many people. In cosmetics it is a harmless thickener.
summary: Salt seasons and preserves food and thickens shampoos. The body needs sodium, but most people eat roughly 50% more than recommended.

physical.phStability: Neutral and stable at all pH values

profile.function: Enhances flavor, controls fermentation in bread, preserves by lowering water activity, and in shampoos thickens surfactant mixtures by packing micelles into worm-like shapes.

reactions.title: Dissociation
reactions.description: Salt separates into sodium and chloride ions in water, which is what the tongue tastes and what nerves use.

reactions.title: Chlor-alkali electrolysis
reactions.description: Electrolysis of brine produces chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide, making salt the starting point for bleach and lye.

mechanisms.title: Nerve and muscle signaling
mechanisms.description: Sodium gradients maintained by the Na+/K+-ATPase pump power nerve impulses and nutrient transport.

mechanisms.title: Blood pressure
mechanisms.description: Excess sodium increases fluid volume and vascular resistance in salt-sensitive people, raising blood pressure.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe; FDA issued voluntary sodium-reduction targets for processed foods in 2021.
Recommends under 2 g of sodium (5 g of salt) per day for adults.
Limit sodium to under 2,300 mg per day for ages 14 and up.

toxicology.mechanism: Very large acute doses cause hypernatremia, drawing water out of brain cells. Chronic excess contributes to hypertension, stroke and kidney disease risk.
toxicology.dosage: Harm from a single product is unlikely; what matters is the daily total. Processed and restaurant foods supply about 70% of dietary sodium in the U.S.

profile.sensitization: Not an allergen. Concentrated salt can sting cuts or irritated skin.

myths.claim: Sea salt and pink Himalayan salt are healthier than table salt.
myths.consensus: By weight they contain about the same sodium; trace minerals are negligible, and they usually lack the iodine added to table salt.

myths.claim: Salt in shampoo damages hair.
myths.consensus: At the 1–2% used for thickening, sodium chloride is not shown to harm hair; the idea mostly comes from marketing for salt-free products.

synthesis.method: Naturally extracted from the sea or underground deposits.
steps: Solar evaporation of seawater in shallow ponds, or
Mining of rock salt deposits, or
Solution mining: water is pumped into salt beds and the brine is evaporated in vacuum pans.
Iodine (as potassium iodide) and anti-caking agents may be added.

environment.persistence: Chloride does not break down and accumulates in fresh water.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Road-salt runoff raises chloride levels that can harm freshwater organisms.

fun.history: Salt was so valuable that it funded empires and wars; Gandhi's 1930 Salt March against the British salt tax became a turning point in India's independence movement.
uses: De-icing roads (the largest use in the U.S.)
Feedstock for chlorine and PVC plastic
fun.occurrence: Seawater holds about 35 g of dissolved salts per liter, most of it sodium chloride.

name: Citric Acid
scoreRationale: A natural metabolite with an exceptional safety record; the main caveat is enamel erosion from frequent acidic drinks.
summary: Citric acid gives lemons their sourness. Made by fermentation, it adds tartness, adjusts pH and captures metal ions in foods, cosmetics and descalers.

physical.solubility: Very soluble in water; soluble in ethanol

profile.function: Adds tartness, lowers pH to help preservatives work, chelates metals that would otherwise catalyze spoilage, and dissolves limescale in cleaners.

reactions.title: Neutralization with baking soda
reactions.description: The fizz in bath bombs and effervescent tablets is citric acid reacting with sodium bicarbonate.

reactions.title: Chelation of metal ions
reactions.description: Its three carboxylate groups wrap around Ca2+, Mg2+, Fe3+ and Cu2+, softening water and stopping metals from catalyzing oxidation (an antioxidant synergist).

reactions.title: Descaling
reactions.description: Converts insoluble calcium carbonate scale into soluble calcium citrate.

mechanisms.title: Krebs cycle intermediate
mechanisms.description: Citrate is made and consumed in the mitochondria of every aerobic cell, so dietary citric acid enters normal energy metabolism.

mechanisms.title: Skin exfoliation
mechanisms.description: As an alpha-hydroxy acid at low pH it loosens bonds between surface skin cells, though it is used mostly as a pH adjuster at low concentrations.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe with no limit beyond good manufacturing practice.
Authorized as E330 at quantum satis (no numerical limit).
Acceptable daily intake "not limited".
Safe in cosmetics in the present practices of use and concentration.

toxicology.mechanism: Concentrated citric acid is an eye and skin irritant because low pH denatures surface proteins; frequent acidic drinks gradually dissolve tooth enamel.
toxicology.dosage: Foods and cosmetics use roughly 0.1–1%. The body processes grams per day through normal metabolism; lemon juice itself is about 5–6% citric acid.

profile.sensitization: Not a sensitizer. It can sting on broken or very sensitive skin at low pH.

myths.claim: Citric acid is made from toxic black mold.
myths.consensus: It is produced by fermenting sugar with Aspergillus niger, then purified; the final crystals contain no mold. A 2018 case series suggested reactions to residual impurities, but controlled studies have not confirmed this.

myths.claim: "Citric acid" on a label means the product contains citrus.
myths.consensus: Industrial citric acid comes from fermentation, not fruit, so it is generally safe for people with citrus allergies.

synthesis.method: Bio-fermented: submerged fermentation of glucose, sucrose or molasses by Aspergillus niger.
steps: The mold is grown in a sugar solution with limited iron and manganese so it overproduces citrate.
The broth is filtered and citric acid is precipitated with lime as calcium citrate.
Sulfuric acid regenerates citric acid, leaving calcium sulfate (gypsum).
The solution is purified with activated carbon and ion exchange, then crystallized.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Low; it is a preferred "green" alternative to phosphates and EDTA in detergents.

fun.history: Carl Wilhelm Scheele first crystallized citric acid from lemon juice in 1784. In 1917 food chemist James Currie discovered that Aspergillus niger makes it efficiently, and Pfizer began industrial production two years later.
uses: Sodium citrate keeps donated blood from clotting
fun.occurrence: Lemons and limes, plus smaller amounts in oranges, berries and tomatoes.

name: Ascorbic Acid
scoreRationale: An essential vitamin with a wide safety margin; very high supplement doses can upset the stomach.
summary: Vitamin C is an essential nutrient and antioxidant. In food it prevents browning; in serums it brightens skin and supports collagen.

physical.solubility: Freely soluble in water; poorly soluble in oils
physical.phStability: Most stable below pH 3.5; oxidizes quickly in air, light and heat

profile.function: Stops cut fruit and cured meats from discoloring, strengthens bread dough, fortifies foods, and in skincare acts as an antioxidant and brightening active.

reactions.title: Oxidation to dehydroascorbic acid
reactions.description: Vitamin C donates two electrons, neutralizing free radicals and reactive oxygen species; this is also why serums turn yellow-brown with age.

reactions.title: Iron reduction
reactions.description: Reduces ferric iron (Fe3+) to ferrous iron (Fe2+), the form the gut absorbs.

mechanisms.title: Collagen synthesis
mechanisms.description: A required cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase enzymes; without it collagen is unstable, which causes scurvy.

mechanisms.title: Skin brightening
mechanisms.description: Interferes with tyrosinase activity and melanin formation, fading hyperpigmentation at effective topical concentrations (typically 10–20% at low pH).

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe as a nutrient and preservative.
RDA 90 mg/day for men and 75 mg/day for women; tolerable upper intake level 2,000 mg/day.
Authorized as E300 at quantum satis.

toxicology.mechanism: Unabsorbed vitamin C draws water into the gut (osmotic diarrhea). In susceptible people, high doses raise urinary oxalate and kidney-stone risk.
toxicology.dosage: Dietary and cosmetic amounts are far below the 2 g/day upper limit. Topical products at 10–20% can tingle because of their low pH.

profile.sensitization: True allergy is very rare. Low-pH serums may cause temporary stinging or redness.

myths.claim: Megadoses of vitamin C prevent colds.
myths.consensus: Cochrane reviews find regular supplements do not reduce how often the general population catches colds, though they slightly shorten their duration.

myths.claim: Vitamin C serum makes skin more sensitive to the sun.
myths.consensus: Unlike some acids it does not increase photosensitivity, and it is often paired with sunscreen for added antioxidant protection.

synthesis.method: Synthetically produced from glucose using a combined chemical and fermentation process.
steps: Glucose is hydrogenated to sorbitol.
Gluconobacter bacteria oxidize sorbitol to L-sorbose.
A second fermentation (or chemical oxidation in the older Reichstein process) yields 2-keto-L-gulonic acid.
Acid-catalyzed lactonization forms ascorbic acid, which is crystallized.

environment.persistence: Not persistent; oxidizes rapidly in air and water.

fun.history: In 1747 naval surgeon James Lind showed citrus cured scurvy in one of the first controlled clinical trials. Albert Szent-Györgyi isolated vitamin C in 1928 and won the 1937 Nobel Prize; Norman Haworth synthesized it in 1933.
uses: Keeping cut apples and avocados from browning
fun.occurrence: Kakadu plums and acerola cherries are the richest sources; citrus, bell peppers and broccoli are everyday ones.

name: Sodium Benzoate
scoreRationale: Well studied and low in toxicity, but it can form trace benzene with vitamin C under heat and light, and it was part of the additive mix linked to hyperactivity in some children.
summary: Sodium benzoate stops mold and yeast in acidic foods, drinks and cosmetics. It's considered safe at permitted levels, with a few chemistry caveats worth knowing.

physical.solubility: Very soluble in water (about 630 g/L); slightly soluble in ethanol

profile.function: Prevents yeast and mold spoilage in sodas, pickles, sauces and rinse-off cosmetics, extending shelf life once a product is opened.

reactions.title: Conversion to benzoic acid
reactions.description: In acidic products, benzoate picks up a proton to form undissociated benzoic acid, the form that crosses microbial membranes.

reactions.title: Benzene formation
reactions.description: With ascorbic acid and trace copper or iron, hydroxyl radicals can decarboxylate benzoate into benzene, accelerated by heat and light. Reformulation has kept most drinks below drinking-water limits.

mechanisms.title: Antimicrobial action
mechanisms.description: Benzoic acid diffuses into microbes, releases its proton in the neutral cytoplasm, acidifies the cell and inhibits glycolytic enzymes such as phosphofructokinase.

mechanisms.title: Human metabolism
mechanisms.description: The liver conjugates benzoate with glycine to form hippuric acid, which is excreted in urine within hours; this pathway is used medically to remove excess nitrogen.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe as a preservative.
Group acceptable daily intake of 0–5 mg/kg body weight (as benzoic acid).
Permitted preservative.
Was included in the Southampton additive mixture; the EU hyperactivity warning applies to the six dyes, not to benzoate.

toxicology.mechanism: Very high doses overwhelm the glycine conjugation pathway. The oral LD50 in rats is about 4 g/kg, making it less acutely toxic than table salt.
toxicology.dosage: Typical exposure is well under the ADI (a 60 kg adult's ADI is about 300 mg/day). Beverages usually contain under 0.05%.

profile.sensitization: Rarely causes hives or pseudo-allergic reactions, mostly in people with aspirin sensitivity or chronic urticaria.

myths.claim: Sodium benzoate turns into benzene in your body.
myths.consensus: Benzene can form in the bottle under specific conditions (vitamin C, metals, heat, light), not in the body. The body converts benzoate to hippuric acid.

myths.claim: It causes ADHD.
myths.consensus: The 2007 Southampton study tested it mixed with dyes and found small behavioral effects in some children; the effect couldn't be pinned on benzoate, and it does not cause ADHD.

steps: Toluene is oxidized by air over cobalt or manganese catalysts to benzoic acid.
Benzoic acid is purified by distillation or crystallization.
It is neutralized with sodium hydroxide or sodium carbonate, then dried.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Low toxicity to fish and invertebrates; EPA Safer Choice lists it as low concern.

fun.history: Benzoic acid was distilled from gum benzoin resin in the 16th century; its antifungal power was described by Ernst Salkowski in 1875, and benzoate became one of the first preservatives approved by the FDA.
uses: Potassium benzoate creates the whistle in fireworks
fun.occurrence: Cranberries, lingonberries, cinnamon, cloves and fermented dairy naturally contain benzoic acid.

name: Potassium Sorbate
scoreRationale: One of the gentlest preservatives; the body metabolizes it like a fatty acid. Rare skin reactions keep it from a top score.
summary: Potassium sorbate prevents mold and yeast in cheese, baked goods, wine and cosmetics. It is broken down by the body much like a dietary fat.

physical.phStability: Effective up to about pH 6.5; best below pH 5

profile.function: Inhibits molds and yeasts (less so bacteria) and stops wine from re-fermenting after bottling.

reactions.title: Acid–base equilibrium
reactions.description: In acidic foods sorbate forms undissociated sorbic acid (pKa 4.76), the active antimicrobial form.

reactions.title: Mold decarboxylation
reactions.description: Some resistant molds decarboxylate sorbic acid to 1,3-pentadiene, causing a kerosene-like off-odor in spoiled cheese.

mechanisms.title: Enzyme inhibition
mechanisms.description: Sorbic acid reacts with sulfhydryl groups of microbial enzymes and disrupts membrane transport, halting growth.

mechanisms.title: Human metabolism
mechanisms.description: Oxidized through normal fatty-acid beta-oxidation to carbon dioxide and water.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe as a chemical preservative.
Group ADI of 11 mg/kg body weight per day for sorbic acid and potassium sorbate.
Permitted preservative.

toxicology.mechanism: Low acute toxicity; very high concentrations can irritate skin and eyes.
toxicology.dosage: Foods use about 0.025–0.2%; cosmetics up to 0.6%. Typical intakes are well within the ADI.

profile.sensitization: Occasional contact urticaria or irritation; true allergy is uncommon.

myths.claim: Potassium sorbate is a pesticide.
myths.consensus: It is a food preservative with a fatty-acid-like structure; it is not registered or used as a pesticide.

myths.claim: It damages DNA.
myths.consensus: Some cell studies used concentrations far above food levels; regulatory reviews by EFSA and JECFA found no genotoxic concern at permitted uses.

steps: Ketene reacts with crotonaldehyde to form a polyester intermediate.
Acid hydrolysis releases sorbic acid, which is purified by crystallization.
Neutralization with potassium hydroxide gives potassium sorbate.

fun.history: August Wilhelm von Hofmann isolated sorbic acid from rowanberry oil in 1859; its antimold effect was recognized around 1940.
uses: Stopping wine from re-fermenting in the bottle
Keeping dried fruit soft and mold-free
fun.occurrence: Named after the rowan tree (Sorbus aucuparia), whose berries contain its precursor.

name: High Fructose Corn Syrup
scoreRationale: Metabolically similar to sugar, but it signals sugar-sweetened, ultra-processed products; a major source of added sugar in American diets.
summary: HFCS is a liquid sweetener made from corn starch. It behaves much like table sugar in the body; the real issue is how much added sugar it delivers.

identity.composition: HFCS-42 (42% fructose, ~53% glucose) for foods; HFCS-55 (55% fructose, ~42% glucose) for soft drinks; about 24% water.

profile.function: Sweetens, retains moisture, prevents crystallization and browns well; being liquid it mixes easily into drinks.

reactions.title: Starch hydrolysis
reactions.description: Enzymes (alpha-amylase, then glucoamylase) break corn starch into glucose.

reactions.title: Isomerization
reactions.description: Immobilized glucose isomerase converts part of the glucose into its sweeter isomer, fructose.

mechanisms.title: Hepatic fructose metabolism
mechanisms.description: Fructose bypasses the main regulatory step of glycolysis in the liver; large amounts promote fat synthesis and raise triglycerides.

mechanisms.title: Satiety
mechanisms.description: Liquid sugars are less filling than solid food, making it easy to consume many calories from sweetened drinks.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe; the FDA rejected renaming it "corn sugar" in 2012.
Sold as glucose-fructose syrup or isoglucose; production quotas ended in 2017.

toxicology.mechanism: Not toxic; health effects stem from excessive added-sugar intake (weight gain, type 2 diabetes risk, fatty liver, dental caries).
toxicology.dosage: A 20-oz regular soda can deliver about 65 g of sugar from HFCS, more than the typical daily added-sugar limit.

profile.sensitization: Not an allergen.

myths.claim: HFCS is far worse than table sugar.
myths.consensus: HFCS-55 is 55% fructose versus 50% in sucrose; controlled studies show similar effects at equal doses. The problem is total added sugar.

myths.claim: HFCS contains mercury.
myths.consensus: A 2009 report found traces in some samples from older chlor-alkali caustic soda; manufacturers use mercury-free processes.

synthesis.method: Semi-synthetic: enzymatic processing of corn starch.
steps: Corn is wet-milled to separate starch.
Alpha-amylase and glucoamylase convert starch to a glucose syrup.
Glucose isomerase converts about 42% of glucose to fructose.
Chromatography enriches fructose to 90%, which is blended back to make HFCS-55.

environment.notes: Tied to large-scale corn monoculture and fertilizer runoff.

fun.history: Japanese researcher Yoshiyuki Takasaki developed an industrial glucose-isomerase process in the 1960s; HFCS replaced sugar in most U.S. sodas by the mid-1980s.
uses: Feed for honeybee colonies in winter
fun.occurrence: Not natural, but honey has a similar fructose-to-glucose ratio.

name: Aspartame
scoreRationale: Safe for most people within the ADI, but IARC's 2023 "possibly carcinogenic" classification, the phenylalanine warning and the WHO advice against sweeteners for weight control keep it in the middle.
summary: Aspartame is a low-calorie sweetener about 200 times sweeter than sugar. Regulators consider it safe within daily limits, but people with PKU must avoid it.

physical.phStability: Most stable at pH 4.3; breaks down with heat or in neutral/alkaline conditions

profile.function: Provides sugar-like sweetness with almost no calories in diet sodas, yogurts, gum and tabletop sweeteners.

reactions.title: Digestive hydrolysis
reactions.description: Gut enzymes split aspartame into aspartic acid, phenylalanine and methanol, which are absorbed like the same compounds from other foods.

reactions.title: Cyclization on heating
reactions.description: Heat and storage convert it to diketopiperazine, which is not sweet, so diet drinks lose sweetness over time.

mechanisms.title: Sweet-taste receptor
mechanisms.description: Binds the T1R2/T1R3 sweet receptor on the tongue.

mechanisms.title: Phenylalanine load
mechanisms.description: People with phenylketonuria (PKU) cannot metabolize phenylalanine, so products must carry a "Phenylketonurics: contains phenylalanine" warning.

regulatory.status: Approved as a general-purpose sweetener.
Reaffirmed the ADI of 40 mg/kg body weight after reviewing cancer data.
Group 2B "possibly carcinogenic to humans" based on limited evidence; a hazard label, not a measure of risk at normal intake.
Conditionally advises against non-sugar sweeteners for long-term weight control.

toxicology.mechanism: Proposed mechanisms from animal and observational studies (oxidative stress, tumors in lifetime rodent studies) have not been consistently confirmed; the Ramazzini rat studies remain contested.
toxicology.dosage: A 70 kg adult would need about 9–14 cans of diet soda every day to reach JECFA's ADI. The methanol from a can is less than from a glass of fruit juice.

profile.sensitization: Not a skin sensitizer. Some people report headaches; controlled trials show inconsistent results.

myths.claim: Aspartame is proven to cause cancer.
myths.consensus: IARC's 2B label means limited evidence (the same category as aloe vera extract). JECFA found no reason to change the safe daily limit.

myths.claim: Aspartame turns into formaldehyde and poisons you.
myths.consensus: Methanol from aspartame is metabolized like the larger amounts naturally present in fruits and vegetables.

synthesis.method: Synthetically manufactured from two amino acids.
steps: L-phenylalanine is esterified with methanol.
It is coupled to L-aspartic acid chemically (with protecting groups) or enzymatically with thermolysin.
The dipeptide ester is purified and crystallized.

fun.history: Chemist James Schlatter discovered aspartame's sweetness by accident in 1965 when he licked his finger while working on an anti-ulcer drug at G.D. Searle.
uses: Flavor-enhancing chewing gum (it prolongs fruit flavors)
fun.occurrence: Synthetic, but built from two amino acids found in all dietary protein.

name: Sucralose
scoreRationale: Approved and mostly unabsorbed, but emerging research on gut microbes, a genotoxic impurity and heating by-products warrants caution.
summary: Sucralose is a chlorinated sugar about 600 times sweeter than sugar. Most of it passes through the body unchanged; newer studies raise open questions.

physical.phStability: Stable over a wide pH range and during most cooking

profile.function: Adds zero-calorie sweetness to drinks, baked goods, protein powders and flavored lip products.

reactions.title: Selective chlorination
reactions.description: Three hydroxyl groups of sucrose are replaced with chlorine, which blocks digestion and boosts sweetness about 600-fold.

reactions.title: Thermal breakdown
reactions.description: Above about 120 °C, especially with glycerol or fats, sucralose can form chlorinated compounds such as chloropropanols; Germany's BfR advises against baking with it at high heat.

mechanisms.title: Minimal absorption
mechanisms.description: About 85% passes through the gut unabsorbed and is excreted; the absorbed fraction leaves in urine.

mechanisms.title: Gut microbiome
mechanisms.description: Some human and animal studies report changes in gut bacteria and glucose responses; results are inconsistent.

regulatory.status: Approved as a general-purpose sweetener (1999).
Authorized as E955.
Conditionally advises against non-sugar sweeteners for weight control.

toxicology.mechanism: A 2023 in-vitro study reported that sucralose-6-acetate, a manufacturing impurity and gut metabolite, damaged DNA in cells; this has not yet been confirmed in humans.
toxicology.dosage: A packet of Splenda contains about 12 mg of sucralose; typical intakes are far below the ADI.

profile.sensitization: Not a known skin sensitizer.

myths.claim: Sucralose is basically sugar, so it's natural.
myths.consensus: It starts as sugar but is chemically chlorinated; the body does not recognize it as sugar.

myths.claim: Zero-calorie sweeteners spike insulin just like sugar.
myths.consensus: Most trials show no acute blood-sugar spike; some show subtle changes in insulin response when combined with carbohydrates.

steps: The 6-hydroxyl of sucrose is protected by acetylation.
Chlorination (for example with a Vilsmeier-type reagent) replaces three hydroxyls with chlorine.
The protecting acetate is removed and the product is crystallized.

environment.persistence: Highly persistent; passes through wastewater treatment largely intact.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Low acute toxicity, but it is now widespread in rivers and groundwater.

fun.history: Discovered in 1976 at Queen Elizabeth College, London, reportedly when a student misheard "test this compound" as "taste this compound".
uses: Tracer for wastewater in groundwater studies
fun.occurrence: Synthetic; not found in nature.

name: Caffeine
scoreRationale: Moderate intake is safe for most adults, but it is a psychoactive stimulant with sensitivity, sleep, pregnancy and overdose caveats.
summary: Caffeine is the world's most widely used stimulant. Up to about 400 mg a day is fine for most healthy adults; energy drinks can pack a lot of it.

physical.solubility: Moderately soluble in water (about 22 g/L), highly soluble in hot water

profile.function: Adds bitterness and stimulant effect to colas and energy drinks; in eye creams it constricts blood vessels to reduce puffiness temporarily.

reactions.title: Supercritical CO2 extraction
reactions.description: Pressurized carbon dioxide selectively dissolves caffeine from green coffee beans in decaffeination.

reactions.title: Liver demethylation
reactions.description: CYP1A2 removes methyl groups, producing paraxanthine, theobromine and theophylline.

mechanisms.title: Adenosine receptor blockade
mechanisms.description: Caffeine blocks A1 and A2A adenosine receptors, preventing the drowsiness signal and increasing dopamine and norepinephrine activity.

mechanisms.title: Half-life
mechanisms.description: Its half-life is about 3–7 hours, longer in pregnancy or with some medications.

regulatory.status: GRAS in cola-type beverages; FDA cites 400 mg/day as not generally associated with adverse effects for healthy adults.
Single doses up to 200 mg and 400 mg/day are safe for adults; 200 mg/day in pregnancy.
Drinks over 150 mg/L must state "High caffeine content" and that they are not recommended for children or pregnant women.

toxicology.mechanism: At high doses it causes rapid heart rate, anxiety and arrhythmia; massive doses (grams) can cause seizures and death, usually from pure powders or pills.
toxicology.dosage: A cup of coffee has about 95 mg; a 16-oz energy drink 150–300 mg. Toxic effects appear around 1.2 g taken quickly; a teaspoon of pure powder can exceed that.

profile.sensitization: Not a skin sensitizer.

myths.claim: Coffee dehydrates you.
myths.consensus: Moderate habitual intake has only a mild diuretic effect; caffeinated drinks still count toward daily fluids.

myths.claim: Caffeine stunts growth.
myths.consensus: There is no evidence that caffeine affects height.

synthesis.method: Mostly naturally extracted (a by-product of decaffeination); also synthesized.
steps: Green coffee beans or tea leaves are extracted with water, CO2 or solvent.
Caffeine is recovered, purified by recrystallization or sublimation.
Synthetic caffeine is made from dimethylurea and malonic acid via the Traube purine synthesis.

environment.persistence: Moderately persistent; a common marker of human wastewater in rivers.

fun.history: Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge isolated caffeine in 1819 after Goethe urged him to analyze coffee beans; Emil Fischer synthesized it in 1895.
uses: Treating breathing pauses in premature babies (caffeine citrate)
fun.occurrence: Coffee, tea, cacao, guarana, yerba mate and kola nut; plants use it to deter insects.

name: Phosphoric Acid
scoreRationale: Safe as used, but frequent colas are linked to enamel erosion and, in women, lower bone density; concentrated forms in cleaners are corrosive.
summary: Phosphoric acid gives colas their tang and powers rust removers. It's fine in moderation, but acidic sodas are hard on teeth.

profile.function: Provides sharp acidity in colas, adjusts pH in cosmetics, and converts rust in toilet and metal cleaners.

reactions.title: Rust conversion
reactions.description: Converts iron oxide into a hard iron phosphate layer that can be painted over.

reactions.title: Neutralization
reactions.description: Reacts with bases to form phosphate buffers used throughout food and cosmetic formulation.

mechanisms.title: Enamel erosion
mechanisms.description: Colas at pH about 2.5 dissolve hydroxyapatite in enamel when sipped frequently.

mechanisms.title: Bone mineral balance
mechanisms.description: A high phosphorus intake with low calcium may disturb calcium balance; cola intake was linked to lower hip bone density in women in the Framingham Osteoporosis Study.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
Authorized as E338 with maximum levels by food category; EFSA set a group ADI for phosphates in 2019.
Danger: causes severe skin burns and eye damage (H314) when concentrated.

toxicology.mechanism: Concentrated acid denatures and hydrolyzes tissue proteins, causing chemical burns.
toxicology.dosage: Colas contain about 0.05%. Rust removers and toilet cleaners can contain 10–30%, requiring gloves and ventilation.

profile.sensitization: Not a sensitizer; concentrated solutions are corrosive.

myths.claim: A cola will dissolve a tooth overnight.
myths.consensus: Erosion takes repeated exposure over time; saliva buffers acids between sips.

myths.claim: Phosphoric acid in soda leaches calcium from your bones.
myths.consensus: The bone link is modest and may partly reflect cola replacing milk in the diet.

steps: Wet process: phosphate rock is digested with sulfuric acid, producing phosphoric acid and gypsum.
Thermal process (food grade): elemental phosphorus is burned to P4O10, then absorbed in water.
equations: Ca5(PO4)3F + 5 H2SO4 + 10 H2O → 3 H3PO4 + 5 CaSO4·2H2O + HF

environment.aquaticToxicity: Phosphate runoff drives algal blooms; phosphates were phased out of U.S. laundry and dishwasher detergents for this reason.

fun.history: Phosphorus was discovered in 1669 by Hennig Brand, who boiled down about 1,500 gallons of urine hunting for the philosopher's stone.
fun.occurrence: Phosphate minerals (apatite); phosphate groups form the backbone of DNA.

name: Monosodium Glutamate
scoreRationale: Decades of controlled research find no consistent harm at normal intakes; it contains a third of the sodium of table salt.
summary: MSG adds savory umami flavor. It's chemically the same glutamate found in tomatoes and parmesan, and controlled studies don't support the old "MSG symptom" fears.

profile.function: Boosts savory, meaty (umami) flavor in soups, snacks, sauces and seasonings, allowing less salt overall.

reactions.title: Dissociation
reactions.description: In food and saliva MSG separates into sodium and free glutamate, the form that activates taste receptors.

mechanisms.title: Umami taste receptor
mechanisms.description: Glutamate binds the T1R1/T1R3 receptor and metabotropic glutamate receptors on the tongue.

mechanisms.title: Gut metabolism
mechanisms.description: Most dietary glutamate is used as fuel by intestinal cells, so little reaches the bloodstream or brain.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe; must be labeled as monosodium glutamate.
ADI "not specified" (the safest category).
Group ADI of 30 mg/kg body weight per day for glutamates.

toxicology.mechanism: No toxic mechanism at dietary levels; very large doses without food may cause transient symptoms in a small number of people.
toxicology.dosage: Typical intake is about 0.5–1 g/day. Symptoms in some trials appeared only after 3 g or more without food.

profile.sensitization: Not an allergen.

myths.claim: "Chinese Restaurant Syndrome" proves MSG is harmful.
myths.consensus: The idea began with a 1968 letter to a medical journal; double-blind studies have not reproduced consistent reactions, and the narrative carried xenophobic undertones.

myths.claim: MSG is artificial.
myths.consensus: It is made by fermentation, and the glutamate is identical to that in tomatoes, parmesan, mushrooms and breast milk.

steps: Corynebacterium glutamicum ferments sugar or starch and secretes glutamic acid.
Glutamic acid is crystallized from the broth.
It is neutralized with sodium hydroxide or carbonate and recrystallized as MSG.

fun.history: Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda isolated glutamate from kombu seaweed broth in 1908, named its taste "umami" and co-founded Ajinomoto to sell it.
fun.occurrence: Parmesan, tomatoes, soy sauce, kombu, mushrooms and human breast milk.

name: Red 40
scoreRationale: Legal and within ADI for most people, but linked to hyperactivity in some children, carries an EU warning label, and is being phased out of U.S. school foods.
summary: Red 40 is the most-used synthetic food dye in the U.S. It's purely cosmetic, and evidence that it affects some children's behavior is driving new restrictions.

physical.phStability: Stable across food pH; resists light and heat

profile.function: Colors candy, drinks, cereals, snacks and cosmetics a bright, consistent red with no flavor or nutritional role.

reactions.title: Azo reduction by gut bacteria
reactions.description: Bacterial azoreductases cleave the azo bond, releasing two sulfonated aromatic amines that are mostly excreted.

mechanisms.title: Behavioral effects in children
mechanisms.description: A 2007 randomized trial (the Southampton study) found mixtures containing Red 40 increased hyperactive behavior in the general child population; California's 2021 OEHHA review reached a similar conclusion.

mechanisms.title: Gut inflammation in animal models
mechanisms.description: A 2022 mouse study found chronic Red 40 exposure raised gut serotonin and worsened experimental colitis; human relevance is unknown.

regulatory.status: Certified color additive; FDA announced in 2025 a plan to phase out petroleum-based dyes, relying largely on industry commitments.
Authorized as E129 but foods must carry the warning "may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children".
The School Food Safety Act (2024) bans Red 40 in public-school foods from the end of 2027.
ADI 0–7 mg/kg body weight.

toxicology.mechanism: Low acute toxicity. Concerns center on neurobehavioral effects in sensitive children and on trace carcinogenic impurities (benzidine) limited by FDA batch certification.
toxicology.dosage: U.S. children's intakes can approach several mg/kg on high-candy days; average intakes are below the ADI.

profile.sensitization: Rare hives or allergic-type reactions reported; not a common sensitizer.

myths.claim: Red 40 is made from bugs.
myths.consensus: That's carmine (cochineal). Red 40 is synthesized from petroleum-derived chemicals.

myths.claim: Red 40 causes ADHD.
myths.consensus: It doesn't cause ADHD, but evidence suggests it can worsen hyperactive behavior in some sensitive children.

steps: Cresidine-4-sulfonic acid is diazotized with nitrous acid at low temperature.
The diazonium salt is coupled with 6-hydroxy-2-naphthalenesulfonic acid (Schaeffer's salt).
The dye is salted out, purified, and each batch is certified by the FDA.

environment.persistence: Moderately persistent; azo dyes resist aerobic breakdown.

fun.history: Introduced in 1971 by Allied Chemical, Red 40 took over after Red No. 2 (amaranth) was banned in the U.S. in 1976.
fun.occurrence: Synthetic only.

name: Yellow 5
scoreRationale: Must be named on U.S. labels due to intolerance reactions, carries the EU hyperactivity warning, and is included in new school-food bans.
summary: Yellow 5 is a synthetic lemon-yellow dye. A small number of people react to it, and it's part of the dye group linked to hyperactivity in some children.

physical.phStability: Stable in acidic foods; good light fastness

profile.function: Colors soft drinks, candies, chips, pickles, soaps and cosmetics yellow or, mixed with blue, green.

reactions.title: Azo reduction
reactions.description: Gut bacteria split tartrazine into sulfanilic acid and an aminopyrazolone that are largely excreted.

mechanisms.title: Intolerance reactions
mechanisms.description: In a small subset of people, especially those sensitive to aspirin, it can trigger hives or asthma through non-IgE (pseudo-allergic) pathways.

mechanisms.title: Behavioral effects
mechanisms.description: Included in the Southampton trial mixtures that increased hyperactivity in some children.

regulatory.status: Certified color; must be declared by name on labels because of intolerance reports.
Authorized as E102 with the mandatory hyperactivity warning label.
Banned in public-school foods from the end of 2027 (AB 2316).

toxicology.mechanism: Low acute toxicity; the main documented hazards are intolerance reactions and behavioral effects in sensitive children.
toxicology.dosage: JECFA ADI is 0–10 mg/kg body weight; typical exposure is lower.

profile.sensitization: Can cause urticaria in sensitive individuals; estimated to affect well under 1 in 1,000 people.

myths.claim: Yellow 5 lowers sperm count.
myths.consensus: This long-running rumor about neon sodas has no supporting human evidence.

myths.claim: Yellow 5 is banned in Europe.
myths.consensus: It is permitted in the EU, but products must carry a warning about children's activity and attention.

steps: Sulfanilic acid is diazotized with nitrous acid.
The diazonium salt is coupled with a sulfophenyl pyrazolone carboxylic acid.
The trisodium salt is isolated, purified and batch-certified.

fun.history: Discovered in 1884 by Swiss chemist Johann Heinrich Ziegler; its name comes from tartaric acid, used in early syntheses.
fun.occurrence: Synthetic only.

name: Caramel Color
scoreRationale: Plain caramel (class I) is benign, but ammonia-process caramels (classes III/IV, used in colas) contain 4-MEI, a possible carcinogen now kept low under California rules.
summary: Caramel color gives colas, sauces and gravies their brown hue. Most types are harmless; the ammonia-made kinds contain a by-product regulators limit.

identity.composition: Complex mixture of polymers from heated carbohydrates. Class I (plain), II (caustic sulfite), III (ammonia) and IV (sulfite-ammonia).

physical.phStability: Classes are matched to product pH (class IV for acidic colas)

profile.function: Provides consistent brown color in colas, soy sauce, beer, gravy, baked goods and some hair and skin products.

reactions.title: Caramelization
reactions.description: Controlled heating of sugars dehydrates and polymerizes them into brown melanoidins and caramelans.

reactions.title: Ammonia process by-product
reactions.description: In classes III and IV, ammonia reacts with sugar fragments to form 4-methylimidazole (4-MEI).

mechanisms.title: 4-MEI in animal studies
mechanisms.description: High doses of 4-MEI caused lung tumors in mice in a U.S. National Toxicology Program study; IARC classified 4-MEI as possibly carcinogenic (Group 2B).

regulatory.status: Color additive exempt from certification.
4-MEI is listed; beverages over 29 µg/day exposure need a warning, which led major colas to reduce 4-MEI levels in 2012.
Set ADIs of 100–300 mg/kg body weight depending on class.

toxicology.mechanism: Caramel itself is poorly absorbed; concern is limited to 4-MEI and a related impurity (THI) in ammonia-process classes.
toxicology.dosage: Exposure depends heavily on cola consumption; reformulated U.S. colas contain much lower 4-MEI than before 2012.

profile.sensitization: Not a known allergen.

myths.claim: Caramel color is just burnt sugar.
myths.consensus: Class I is, but classes III and IV are made with ammonia compounds that create by-products like 4-MEI.

synthesis.method: Semi-synthetic: controlled heating of food-grade carbohydrates.
steps: Glucose or sucrose syrup is heated with food-grade acids, alkalis or salts.
Ammonium or sulfite compounds are added for classes II–IV to tune color and charge.
The mixture is cooled and filtered when target color intensity is reached.

fun.history: Caramel is among the oldest food colorings, used in beer and spirits since the 1800s.
fun.occurrence: Browning of sugars in cooking creates similar compounds naturally.

name: Xanthan Gum
scoreRationale: Very well tolerated at the tiny amounts used; large doses act as a laxative, and it should not be given to premature infants.
summary: Xanthan gum is a fermentation-made fiber that thickens sauces, dressings, gluten-free baking and lotions using less than 1%.

identity.composition: High-molecular-weight polysaccharide: a cellulose backbone with trisaccharide side chains of mannose and glucuronic acid.

physical.solubility: Dissolves in hot or cold water to form viscous solutions
physical.phStability: Stable from pH 2 to 12 and through heating and freezing

profile.function: Creates viscosity and suspends particles, keeping dressings from separating and replacing gluten's structure in gluten-free baking.

reactions.title: Shear thinning
reactions.description: Its rigid helical chains align under stirring, so sauces pour easily but thicken again at rest.

reactions.title: Synergy with locust bean gum
reactions.description: Its helices bind to galactomannans, forming elastic gels that neither forms alone.

mechanisms.title: Fermentable fiber
mechanisms.description: Human enzymes cannot digest it; gut bacteria ferment part of it, and large doses increase stool bulk.

regulatory.status: Approved food additive.
ADI "not specified"; FDA and EFSA advise against use in premature infants after thickener-associated necrotizing enterocolitis cases.

toxicology.mechanism: Not absorbed; effects are mechanical and fermentative in the gut.
toxicology.dosage: Foods use about 0.05–0.5%. Laxative effects appear above about 15 g/day.

profile.sensitization: Rare occupational allergy from inhaling powder; food reactions are very uncommon.

myths.claim: Xanthan gum is made from bacteria, so it's unsafe.
myths.consensus: Bacteria make it during fermentation, but the purified gum contains no living organisms.

steps: The bacterium ferments glucose or sucrose and secretes xanthan.
The broth is pasteurized to kill the bacteria.
Xanthan is precipitated with isopropyl alcohol, dried and milled.

fun.history: Discovered in the 1950s by Allene Rosalind Jeanes's team at the USDA; approved for food in 1968.
fun.occurrence: Made by the same bacterium that causes black rot on cabbage and broccoli.

name: Soy Lecithin
scoreRationale: A natural phospholipid mixture with a long safety record; trace soy protein matters only for highly sensitive allergy sufferers.
summary: Lecithin is a natural emulsifier from soybean oil that helps oil and water mix in chocolate, dressings and creams.

identity.composition: Mixture of phospholipids (phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylinositol), glycolipids and triglycerides.

physical.solubility: Disperses in water; soluble in oils

profile.function: Stabilizes emulsions, reduces chocolate viscosity, prevents sticking in cooking sprays and softens skin in creams.

reactions.title: Interface stabilization
reactions.description: Its amphiphilic molecules sit at oil–water interfaces, lowering interfacial tension and preventing droplets from merging.

reactions.title: Enzymatic hydrolysis
reactions.description: Phospholipases split lecithin into lysolecithin, a stronger emulsifier used in some processing.

mechanisms.title: Choline source
mechanisms.description: Phosphatidylcholine supplies choline, used for cell membranes and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
ADI "not specified"; no safety concern at reported uses.
Declared as soy under FALCPA because trace soy protein may remain.

toxicology.mechanism: Digested like dietary fats and phospholipids.
toxicology.dosage: Chocolate uses about 0.3–0.5%. Supplement doses of several grams per day are well tolerated.

profile.sensitization: Most soy-allergic people tolerate it, but highly sensitive individuals may react to protein traces.

myths.claim: Soy lecithin disrupts hormones.
myths.consensus: Lecithin contains negligible isoflavones; the phytoestrogen debate concerns whole soy foods and supplements.

synthesis.method: Naturally extracted as a by-product of soybean oil refining.
steps: Crude soybean oil is mixed with water (degumming), hydrating the phospholipids.
The hydrated gums are separated by centrifuge.
The gums are dried, and may be bleached or fractionated.

fun.history: French chemist Théodore Gobley isolated lecithin from egg yolk in the 1840s and named it after the Greek "lekithos" (egg yolk).
fun.occurrence: Egg yolks, soybeans, sunflower seeds and every cell membrane.

name: Sodium Bicarbonate
scoreRationale: Extremely safe at normal uses; only large ingestions (as a home antacid) pose risks.
summary: Baking soda leavens baked goods, neutralizes odors, and scrubs gently. It's one of the safest multi-purpose household chemicals.

profile.function: Releases CO2 to raise dough, neutralizes acids and odors, softens water, and acts as a mild abrasive in toothpaste and cleaners.

reactions.title: Leavening with acid
reactions.description: Acids in buttermilk or baking powder release carbon dioxide bubbles.

reactions.title: Thermal decomposition
reactions.description: Heat alone decomposes it to sodium carbonate, water and CO2.

reactions.title: Reaction with vinegar
reactions.description: Neutralizes acetic acid into sodium acetate, water and CO2.

mechanisms.title: Acid buffering
mechanisms.description: Bicarbonate is the body's main blood buffer; as an antacid it neutralizes stomach acid.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
Authorized as E500(ii) at quantum satis.
Safe as used in cosmetics.

toxicology.mechanism: Large ingestions can cause metabolic alkalosis and high blood sodium; rapid CO2 release after big meals has rarely caused stomach rupture.
toxicology.dosage: Baking uses about 1 teaspoon per recipe. Antacid labels limit adult use to a few grams per day.

profile.sensitization: Not a sensitizer; alkaline deodorants can irritate sensitive underarms.

myths.claim: Baking soda plus vinegar is a super cleaner.
myths.consensus: They neutralize each other into salty water; the fizz is only CO2. Each works better on its own.

myths.claim: Baking soda cures cancer by alkalizing the body.
myths.consensus: Blood pH is tightly regulated; diet cannot meaningfully change it, and this claim has caused harm.

synthesis.method: Mined (from trona or nahcolite) or synthetically manufactured.
steps: Solvay process: brine absorbs ammonia and carbon dioxide, precipitating sodium bicarbonate.
Or trona ore is refined to soda ash, then carbonated to bicarbonate.
The crystals are washed and dried.
equations: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O → NaHCO3 + NH4Cl

environment.persistence: Not persistent; part of the natural carbonate cycle.

fun.history: Commercial baking soda was sold in the U.S. from 1846 by the company later known as Church & Dwight (Arm & Hammer); Ernest Solvay's 1860s process made it cheap.
uses: Blasting paint off delicate surfaces (soda blasting)
fun.occurrence: The mineral nahcolite, mineral springs, and human blood as the bicarbonate buffer.

name: Carrageenan
scoreRationale: Approved worldwide, but ongoing debate about gut inflammation and EFSA's call for more data keep it in the middle.
summary: Carrageenan is a seaweed-derived thickener used in dairy alternatives, deli meats and toothpaste. Its gut effects remain debated.

identity.composition: Sulfated linear galactans (kappa, iota, lambda types) from red seaweeds.

physical.solubility: Soluble in hot water; kappa and iota form gels on cooling

profile.function: Thickens and stabilizes plant milks, ice cream, chocolate milk and deli meats; binds toothpaste.

reactions.title: Ion-induced gelling
reactions.description: Kappa-carrageenan forms firm gels with potassium ions and iota-carrageenan soft gels with calcium, as helices link together.

reactions.title: Acid hydrolysis
reactions.description: Harsh acid and heat break it into low-molecular-weight poligeenan, a different substance not permitted in food.

mechanisms.title: Intestinal inflammation debate
mechanisms.description: Some cell and animal studies link carrageenan to inflammation via TLR4 signaling; other studies and regulatory reviews found no effect at food-grade molecular weights.

regulatory.status: Approved food additive.
Temporary ADI of 75 mg/kg body weight per day while more data are gathered.
Remains allowed after a 2016 advisory board vote to remove it was not adopted.

toxicology.mechanism: Food-grade carrageenan is poorly absorbed; concern focuses on possible degradation to smaller fragments and on gut barrier effects in sensitive people.
toxicology.dosage: Foods use about 0.01–1%. EFSA estimated some high consumers could exceed the temporary ADI.

profile.sensitization: Not a common allergen.

myths.claim: Carrageenan is the same as poligeenan, a carcinogen.
myths.consensus: Poligeenan is a degraded, much smaller molecule; food-grade carrageenan has a specified minimum molecular weight.

steps: Seaweed (Kappaphycus, Eucheuma, Chondrus) is washed and treated with hot alkali.
The extract is filtered and concentrated.
Carrageenan is precipitated with alcohol or potassium chloride, dried and milled.

environment.notes: Seaweed farming supports coastal communities in the Philippines and Indonesia.

fun.history: Irish cooks have thickened milk puddings with Irish moss (Chondrus crispus) for centuries; the name comes from Carragheen, a coastal area of Ireland.
fun.occurrence: Cell walls of red seaweeds.

name: Vitamin E
scoreRationale: An essential nutrient and gentle antioxidant; only high-dose supplements carry risks.
summary: Vitamin E protects oils from going rancid and helps defend skin lipids against oxidation. It's among the safest antioxidants.

physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; soluble in oils and ethanol
physical.phStability: Stable, but oxidizes with light and air

profile.function: Prevents rancidity in oils and cosmetics and provides antioxidant and conditioning benefits for skin.

reactions.title: Chain-breaking antioxidant
reactions.description: Donates a hydrogen atom from its phenol to a lipid peroxyl radical, stopping chain reactions that turn fats rancid.

reactions.title: Regeneration by vitamin C
reactions.description: Ascorbate reduces the tocopheroxyl radical back to tocopherol, recycling it.

mechanisms.title: Membrane protection
mechanisms.description: Embedded in cell membranes, it protects polyunsaturated fatty acids from peroxidation.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe as a nutrient and preservative.
RDA 15 mg/day; upper limit 1,000 mg/day from supplements.
Safe as used in cosmetics.

toxicology.mechanism: High-dose supplements can interfere with vitamin K-dependent clotting; the SELECT trial found 400 IU/day increased prostate cancer risk.
toxicology.dosage: Foods and cosmetics contain milligrams; concerns apply to long-term supplement doses of hundreds of IU per day.

profile.sensitization: Contact dermatitis is uncommon but reported, more often with tocopheryl acetate or linoleate derivatives.

myths.claim: Vitamin E oil erases scars.
myths.consensus: Controlled studies show no benefit over plain moisturizer, and some people develop contact dermatitis.

synthesis.method: Naturally extracted from vegetable oils, or synthesized.
steps: Natural: tocopherols are concentrated from soybean-oil deodorizer distillate by molecular distillation.
Synthetic: trimethylhydroquinone is condensed with isophytol under acid catalysis to all-rac-alpha-tocopherol.

fun.history: Herbert Evans and Katharine Bishop discovered vitamin E in 1922 as a factor rats needed for fertility; the name tocopherol comes from Greek for "to bear offspring".
uses: Stabilizer in plastics for medical implants
fun.occurrence: Wheat germ oil, sunflower seeds, almonds and olive oil.

name: Natural Flavors
scoreRationale: Generally safe, but the blend is undisclosed and can include carriers and processing aids that consumers cannot evaluate.
summary: "Natural flavors" are proprietary blends of flavor chemicals from plant or animal sources. They're usually safe, but you can't see what's inside.

identity.composition: Undisclosed blends of essential oils, extracts, distillates and fermentation products, often with carriers such as ethanol, propylene glycol or maltodextrin.

profile.function: Adds or restores specific tastes and aromas lost in processing, at parts-per-million concentrations.

reactions.title: Extraction and distillation
reactions.description: Volatile aroma compounds are separated from plant or animal sources with steam, solvents or supercritical CO2.

reactions.title: Fermentation and enzymes
reactions.description: Microbes or enzymes can convert natural precursors into flavor molecules and still qualify as natural.

mechanisms.title: Olfaction
mechanisms.description: Volatile molecules activate some of the roughly 400 human olfactory receptor types; most of what we call flavor is smell.

regulatory.status: Defined as flavor derived from plant or animal sources whose primary function is flavor, not nutrition.
Industry-led expert panel reviews flavor substances; critics note limited FDA oversight.

toxicology.mechanism: Individual flavor compounds are used at very low levels; safety depends on the specific undisclosed components.
toxicology.dosage: Typically less than 0.1% of a food.

profile.sensitization: Allergens must still be declared, but people with rare sensitivities cannot identify hidden components.

myths.claim: "Natural flavors" means the product contains that fruit.
myths.consensus: Strawberry natural flavor can be derived from other natural sources; it need not come from strawberries.

myths.claim: Natural flavors are safer than artificial ones.
myths.consensus: Many natural and artificial flavor molecules are chemically identical; the difference is where they come from, not how safe they are.

steps: Raw materials are extracted or distilled to isolate flavor fractions.
Fermentation or enzymatic conversion can produce specific natural flavor molecules.
Flavorists blend dozens of components with carriers into a proprietary formula.

fun.history: The modern flavor industry grew in the 20th century; FEMA's GRAS program began reviewing flavor substances in 1960.
fun.occurrence: Derived from fruits, spices, herbs, meat, dairy and fermentation.

name: Artificial Flavors
scoreRationale: Individually evaluated flavor chemicals at tiny levels, but undisclosed blends and their presence in ultra-processed foods lower the score.
summary: Artificial flavors are synthesized flavor molecules, often identical to natural ones. They're used in tiny amounts but aren't individually listed.

identity.composition: Blends of synthesized flavor molecules (for example vanillin, ethyl butyrate, benzaldehyde) plus carriers.

profile.function: Delivers consistent, affordable flavor profiles that do not depend on crop quality.

reactions.title: Esterification
reactions.description: Fruity esters are made by reacting acids with alcohols, e.g., ethyl butyrate for pineapple.

mechanisms.title: Olfactory receptors
mechanisms.description: Synthetic flavor molecules bind the same odorant receptors as their natural twins.

regulatory.status: Permitted synthetic flavoring substances are listed in federal regulations; others are GRAS through FEMA review.
Removed seven synthetic flavors, including pulegone and benzophenone, from the permitted list.

toxicology.mechanism: Varies by molecule; most are simple esters, aldehydes and alcohols metabolized quickly.
toxicology.dosage: Usually parts per million.

profile.sensitization: Rare; cinnamaldehyde and some aldehydes can sensitize in cosmetics.

myths.claim: Artificial flavors are made in labs, so they must be worse.
myths.consensus: Synthetic vanillin is the same molecule as vanillin from vanilla beans.

steps: Target flavor molecules are synthesized from petrochemical or other feedstocks.
They are purified and blended with carriers by flavorists.

fun.history: Ferdinand Tiemann and Wilhelm Haarmann synthesized vanillin in 1874, launching the synthetic flavor industry.
fun.occurrence: Many of the same molecules occur in fruits and spices.

name: Titanium Dioxide
scoreRationale: An effective, well-tolerated sunscreen filter on skin, but banned as a food additive in the EU over unresolved genotoxicity concerns, and its powder is a possible carcinogen when inhaled.
summary: Titanium dioxide is a bright white mineral pigment and sunscreen filter. On skin it's protective; in food and inhaled powders it's under scrutiny.

profile.function: Makes candy coatings, frosting and toothpaste opaque white; in sunscreen it reflects, scatters and absorbs UV light.

reactions.title: Photocatalysis
reactions.description: UV light excites electrons in TiO2, creating electron–hole pairs that generate reactive oxygen species; cosmetic grades are coated with silica or alumina to suppress this.

mechanisms.title: UV attenuation
mechanisms.description: Particles scatter and absorb UVB and short UVA; they stay on the skin surface rather than penetrating intact skin.

mechanisms.title: Gut exposure
mechanisms.description: Food-grade TiO2 includes nanoparticles that can accumulate in some tissues in animal studies; EFSA could not rule out DNA damage.

regulatory.status: No longer considered safe as a food additive; E171 banned in EU food since 2022.
Permitted color additive in food and a sunscreen active ingredient.
regulatory.limit: Up to 1% of food by weight (21 CFR 73.575); up to 25% in sunscreen

regulatory.status: Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic) based on inhalation of powder in rats.

toxicology.mechanism: Inhaled fine particles cause lung inflammation in rats; potential genotoxicity from nanoparticles in food remains unresolved.
toxicology.dosage: In lotions it is not absorbed through intact skin; avoid inhaling loose powders and sprays.

profile.sensitization: Not a skin sensitizer; well tolerated by sensitive skin.

myths.claim: Mineral sunscreens with TiO2 get into your bloodstream.
myths.consensus: Studies show it stays on the skin's surface; FDA absorption concerns focused on chemical filters like oxybenzone.

steps: Chloride process: rutile ore is chlorinated with coke to titanium tetrachloride.
TiCl4 is purified by distillation and burned in oxygen to pure TiO2.
Sulfate process (alternative): ilmenite ore is digested in sulfuric acid.
Particles are milled and coated for cosmetic use.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Low for coated bulk grades; nanoparticle effects are under study.

fun.history: William Gregor discovered titanium in 1791 in Cornish sand; TiO2 replaced toxic lead white in paints from the 1920s.
fun.occurrence: Minerals rutile, anatase and brookite.

name: BHT
scoreRationale: Permitted at low levels, but mixed animal data (tumor promotion and inhibition) and possible endocrine effects keep it under review.
summary: BHT is a synthetic antioxidant that keeps cereals, fats and cosmetics from going rancid. Regulators allow it; some scientists want a fresh look.

physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; soluble in fats and oils

profile.function: Prevents oxidation of fats and oils in cereals, chewing gum and cosmetics.

reactions.title: Radical scavenging
reactions.description: Its hindered phenol donates a hydrogen atom to peroxyl radicals, forming a stable phenoxyl radical.

mechanisms.title: Metabolism
mechanisms.description: Oxidized in the liver by cytochrome P450 enzymes; some metabolites have been studied for toxicity in rodents.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
regulatory.limit: Up to 0.02% of the fat content (21 CFR 182.3173)

regulatory.status: ADI 0.25 mg/kg body weight per day.
Group 3 (not classifiable as to carcinogenicity).

toxicology.mechanism: High doses in rodents affected the liver and thyroid; effects on tumors were both promoting and protective depending on the study.
toxicology.dosage: Human intake is estimated well below the EFSA ADI.

profile.sensitization: Rare contact allergy.

myths.claim: BHT is embalming fluid.
myths.consensus: BHT is an antioxidant; embalming uses formaldehyde. BHT is also used in some fuels and rubbers, which is where the rumor may come from.

steps: p-Cresol is alkylated with isobutylene in the presence of an acid catalyst (Friedel–Crafts alkylation).
The product is purified by distillation and crystallization.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Toxic to aquatic life at higher concentrations.

fun.history: Patented in 1947 and approved for food use in the U.S. in 1954.
fun.occurrence: Has been reported as a natural product of some phytoplankton.

name: Maltodextrin
scoreRationale: Safe, but it is a rapidly digested carbohydrate with a high glycemic index and a hallmark of ultra-processed foods.
summary: Maltodextrin is a starch-derived powder that adds body and carries flavors. It digests quickly into glucose.

identity.composition: Short chains of glucose units (dextrose equivalent below 20) from partial starch hydrolysis.

profile.function: Adds bulk and mouthfeel, carries spray-dried flavors, and supplies quick energy in sports drinks.

reactions.title: Starch hydrolysis
reactions.description: Acid or amylase enzymes cut starch into shorter glucose chains.

mechanisms.title: Rapid digestion
mechanisms.description: Amylases quickly break it down, so its glycemic index can exceed that of table sugar.

mechanisms.title: Gut effects
mechanisms.description: Some animal studies suggest it may alter gut mucus and bacteria; human data are limited.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.

toxicology.mechanism: Not toxic; metabolic effects mirror other rapidly digested carbohydrates.
toxicology.dosage: Usually small amounts; concern is higher in drinks and powders where it is a major ingredient.

profile.sensitization: Not an allergen; wheat-derived versions are gluten-free after processing.

myths.claim: Maltodextrin is worse than sugar.
myths.consensus: Its glycemic index is high, but most foods contain only small amounts.

steps: Corn, potato, rice or wheat starch is gelatinized in water.
Alpha-amylase partially hydrolyzes it.
The solution is purified and spray-dried.

fun.history: Commercialized in the mid-20th century as starch processing matured.
uses: Turning oils into powders in modernist cooking
fun.occurrence: Forms naturally when starch is partly digested.

name: Sodium Nitrite
scoreRationale: Prevents deadly botulism, but in processed meats it forms carcinogenic nitrosamines; processed meat is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen.
summary: Sodium nitrite cures bacon, ham and hot dogs, keeping them pink and safe from botulism. Cooking cured meat can create cancer-causing nitrosamines.

physical.phStability: Forms nitrous acid in acidic conditions

profile.function: Gives cured meats their pink color and flavor and inhibits Clostridium botulinum.

reactions.title: Nitrosylation of myoglobin
reactions.description: Nitrite forms nitric oxide, which binds myoglobin to create pink nitrosylmyoglobin.

reactions.title: Nitrosamine formation
reactions.description: At high heat (such as frying bacon), nitrous acid reacts with amines to form N-nitrosamines; added vitamin C or erythorbate reduces this.

mechanisms.title: Carcinogenicity
mechanisms.description: Nitrosamines are metabolized to DNA-alkylating agents that cause mutations; this underlies the link between processed meat and colorectal cancer.

mechanisms.title: Methemoglobinemia
mechanisms.description: Large doses oxidize hemoglobin to methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen.

regulatory.status: Permitted in cured meats with limits; bacon must include ascorbate or erythorbate.
regulatory.limit: 200 ppm maximum in finished products (21 CFR 172.175)

regulatory.status: Processed meat is Group 1 (carcinogenic); ingested nitrite under conditions causing nitrosation is Group 2A.
Lowered maximum added nitrite levels in meat products.

toxicology.mechanism: Acute toxicity from methemoglobinemia; chronic risk from nitrosamine formation.
toxicology.dosage: Cured meats contain tens of ppm residual nitrite. Most dietary nitrite comes from vegetables' nitrate converted by oral bacteria, which comes with protective antioxidants.

profile.sensitization: Not an allergen.

myths.claim: "Uncured, no nitrates added" bacon is nitrite-free.
myths.consensus: It is cured with celery powder, a natural nitrate source that becomes the same nitrite.

steps: Nitrogen oxides from ammonia oxidation are absorbed into sodium hydroxide or carbonate solution.
Sodium nitrite crystallizes and is separated from nitrate.

environment.persistence: Converted to nitrate in the environment.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Toxic to fish at elevated concentrations.

fun.history: Salt-curing with saltpeter is ancient; in the late 1800s scientists found bacteria convert nitrate to nitrite, the real curing agent. The USDA approved direct nitrite use in 1925.
fun.occurrence: Formed from nitrate in leafy greens and beets by oral bacteria.

name: Palm Oil
scoreRationale: High in saturated fat, refining can create processing contaminants, and unsustainable plantations drive deforestation.
summary: Palm oil is the world's most-used vegetable oil, in foods, soaps and cosmetics. It's versatile but high in saturated fat and linked to deforestation.

identity.composition: Triglycerides with about 44% palmitic, 39% oleic, 10% linoleic and 5% stearic acid.

profile.function: Provides texture and shelf stability in baked goods and spreads, and is the base of soaps and many surfactants.

reactions.title: Saponification
reactions.description: Reacting palm oil with lye makes soap (sodium palmitate) and glycerin.

reactions.title: Refining contaminants
reactions.description: Deodorizing at over 200 °C can form 3-MCPD and glycidyl fatty acid esters; industry has reduced them since EFSA's 2016 opinion.

mechanisms.title: Blood cholesterol
mechanisms.description: Palmitic acid raises LDL cholesterol compared with unsaturated oils.

regulatory.status: Maximum limits for glycidyl esters in vegetable oils since 2018.
The Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil certifies deforestation-controlled supply chains.
Requires proof that palm oil is deforestation-free once it applies.

toxicology.mechanism: Not acutely toxic; long-term risk relates to saturated fat intake and processing contaminants.
toxicology.dosage: Health guidance recommends limiting saturated fat to under 10% of calories.

profile.sensitization: Not an allergen.

myths.claim: Red palm oil is a superfood.
myths.consensus: It is rich in beta-carotene and vitamin E, but it's still about 50% saturated fat.

steps: Fresh fruit bunches are sterilized with steam.
Fruit is pressed to release crude palm oil.
Oil is refined, bleached and deodorized, then fractionated into liquid olein and solid stearin.

environment.notes: Plantation expansion in Indonesia and Malaysia has destroyed rainforest habitat for orangutans and released peatland carbon.

fun.history: West Africans have used palm oil for about 5,000 years; residues have been found in an Egyptian tomb at Abydos.
fun.occurrence: Fruit of the oil palm (Elaeis guineensis).

name: Lactic Acid
scoreRationale: A natural metabolite; in leave-on skincare at higher strengths it can irritate and increases sun sensitivity.
summary: Lactic acid is the tang in yogurt and a gentle exfoliating acid in skincare. It's produced naturally by your own muscles and skin.

profile.function: Acidifies and preserves foods, exfoliates and hydrates skin, and descales in bathroom cleaners.

reactions.title: Lactic fermentation
reactions.description: Bacteria convert sugars into lactic acid, souring milk and vegetables.

reactions.title: Polymerization
reactions.description: Condenses into polylactic acid (PLA), a compostable plastic.

mechanisms.title: Exfoliation
mechanisms.description: At low pH it weakens bonds between surface skin cells, smoothing texture.

mechanisms.title: Hydration
mechanisms.description: Sodium lactate is a component of the skin's natural moisturizing factor, drawing water into the stratum corneum.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe; recommends a sunburn alert on alpha-hydroxy acid cosmetics.
AHAs are safe at 10% or less, pH 3.5 or higher, with sun protection advised.

toxicology.mechanism: Low pH can irritate eyes and skin; AHAs thin the outer skin layer, raising UV sensitivity.
toxicology.dosage: Foods use under 1%; retail skincare typically 5–10%.

profile.sensitization: Not a sensitizer; can sting sensitive skin.

myths.claim: Lactic acid buildup causes next-day muscle soreness.
myths.consensus: Delayed soreness comes from muscle micro-damage; lactate clears within an hour and is used as fuel.

steps: Lactobacillus or engineered microbes ferment glucose or sucrose.
Lactic acid is recovered as calcium lactate and acidified.
It is purified by distillation or ion exchange.

fun.history: Carl Wilhelm Scheele isolated lactic acid from sour milk in 1780.
fun.occurrence: Yogurt, sauerkraut, sourdough, sweat and working muscles.

name: Acesulfame Potassium
scoreRationale: Approved and not metabolized, but long-term human data are thinner than for other sweeteners, it persists in the environment, and WHO discourages sweeteners for weight control.
summary: Ace-K is a zero-calorie sweetener about 200 times sweeter than sugar, often blended with sucralose or aspartame.

profile.function: Sweetens diet drinks and sugar-free foods, masking bitterness when blended with other sweeteners.

reactions.title: Stability
reactions.description: Resists heat and acid, and is excreted unchanged.

mechanisms.title: Sweet taste receptor
mechanisms.description: Activates T1R2/T1R3; at high concentrations it also triggers bitter receptors, causing an aftertaste.

regulatory.status: Approved general-purpose sweetener (2003).
ADI 0–15 mg/kg body weight.

toxicology.mechanism: Not metabolized; animal studies at typical exposures show no consistent toxicity.
toxicology.dosage: Diet sodas contain tens of mg per can, well under the ADI.

profile.sensitization: Not a known sensitizer.

myths.claim: Ace-K is metabolized into toxic acetoacetamide.
myths.consensus: Acetoacetamide forms only after long storage under harsh conditions; the sweetener is excreted unchanged.

steps: Sulfamic acid reacts with diketene to form an acetoacetamide sulfonic acid.
Sulfur trioxide cyclizes the intermediate.
Neutralization with potassium hydroxide gives acesulfame potassium.

environment.persistence: Highly persistent; used as a tracer for wastewater in groundwater.
environment.biodegradability: Poorly biodegradable, though some treatment plants now degrade it.

fun.history: Discovered in 1967 by Karl Clauss at Hoechst, who noticed sweetness after licking his finger.
fun.occurrence: Synthetic only.
