summary: Sodium citrate buffers pH, keeps melted cheese smooth, and softens water in eco-friendly detergents.

profile.function: Buffers acidity in drinks, emulsifies processed cheese, and binds calcium and magnesium in detergents.

reactions.title: Calcium chelation
reactions.description: Binds calcium in casein so cheese proteins disperse smoothly when melted and hard-water ions don't block detergents.

mechanisms.title: Anticoagulation
mechanisms.description: Chelates calcium needed for clotting, which is why it is used in blood collection bags.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
Authorized as E331 at quantum satis.

toxicology.mechanism: Very low toxicity; metabolized to bicarbonate.
toxicology.dosage: Foods use under 1%.

profile.sensitization: Not a sensitizer.

myths.claim: Sodium citrate is just salt.
myths.consensus: It is a citrate salt with far less sodium per gram than table salt and different functions.

synthesis.method: Made by neutralizing fermentation-derived citric acid.
steps: Citric acid is neutralized with sodium hydroxide or carbonate, then crystallized.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Low; a green replacement for phosphate builders.

fun.history: Used as a blood anticoagulant since 1914, making stored blood transfusions practical during World War I.
fun.occurrence: Forms whenever citric acid meets sodium in solution, including in citrus-flavored drinks.

name: Glycerin
scoreRationale: One of the best-studied, gentlest moisturizing ingredients; the only notable caution is very high amounts in slush drinks for young children.
summary: Glycerin draws water into the skin and keeps foods moist. It's a gentle, versatile ingredient found in nearly every moisturizer.

physical.solubility: Miscible with water and alcohol; insoluble in oils

profile.function: Attracts and holds water in the skin's outer layer, softens formulas, keeps baked goods and candies moist, and prevents toothpaste from drying out.

reactions.title: Saponification by-product
reactions.description: Making soap from fats releases glycerin alongside the soap.

reactions.title: Nitration
reactions.description: Glycerin reacts with nitric and sulfuric acids to form nitroglycerin, both an explosive and an angina medicine.

mechanisms.title: Stratum corneum hydration
mechanisms.description: Its hydroxyl groups hydrogen-bond with water; aquaporin-3 channels transport glycerol in the epidermis, supporting hydration and barrier repair.

mechanisms.title: Barrier support
mechanisms.description: Keeps lipids in the skin barrier in a more fluid, functional state in dry conditions.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
Safe as used in cosmetics.
Advises that slush-ice drinks containing glycerol should not be given to children under 4.

toxicology.mechanism: Very low toxicity. Large amounts drunk quickly by small children can cause glycerol intoxication (low blood sugar, shock).
toxicology.dosage: Cosmetics use about 2–10%; the oral LD50 in rats exceeds 12 g/kg.

profile.sensitization: Essentially non-sensitizing.

myths.claim: Glycerin pulls moisture out of your skin.
myths.consensus: In extremely dry air, pure glycerin could draw water from deeper skin, but at typical 3–10% in formulas it hydrates skin.

myths.claim: Vegetable glycerin is healthier than synthetic glycerin.
myths.consensus: They are the same molecule; source matters for sustainability and dietary preferences, not safety.

synthesis.method: Mostly a by-product of biodiesel and soap making (plant or animal fats); also synthesized from propylene.
steps: Triglycerides are transesterified with methanol (biodiesel) or saponified with lye (soap).
The glycerin-rich phase is separated.
Crude glycerin is neutralized, distilled and bleached to USP grade.

fun.history: Carl Wilhelm Scheele discovered glycerin in 1779 by heating olive oil with lead oxide and called it the "sweet principle of fat".
uses: Nitroglycerin for dynamite and heart medicine
fun.occurrence: The backbone of every fat and oil molecule.

name: Sodium Lauryl Sulfate
scoreRationale: Not carcinogenic, but a well-documented skin irritant that strips barrier lipids; better tolerated in rinse-off products than leave-on.
summary: SLS is a powerful foaming cleanser in shampoos, toothpastes and cleaners. It's safe but can irritate sensitive skin and mouths.

physical.solubility: Soluble in water; forms micelles above about 8 mM
physical.phStability: Stable pH 4–10; hydrolyzes in strong acid

profile.function: Lowers surface tension so water can lift oils and dirt, and creates rich foam.

reactions.title: Micelle formation
reactions.description: Above its critical micelle concentration, SLS molecules cluster with tails inward, trapping oils in their cores.

reactions.title: Protein denaturation
reactions.description: Binds and unfolds proteins, the basis of SDS-PAGE lab analysis and of its irritancy.

mechanisms.title: Barrier disruption
mechanisms.description: Extracts stratum corneum lipids and binds keratin, increasing water loss and letting irritants in; it is the standard reference irritant in dermatology research.

mechanisms.title: Oral mucosa
mechanisms.description: In toothpaste it may disrupt the protective mucin layer; some trials show SLS-free toothpaste reduces canker sores in people prone to them.

regulatory.status: Safe in rinse-off products; leave-on products should contain no more than 1%.
Permitted as a direct food additive, e.g., as a whipping aid for egg whites.
Listed among safer surfactants for cleaning products.

toxicology.mechanism: Irritation from lipid extraction and protein denaturation; not genotoxic or carcinogenic.
toxicology.dosage: Shampoos contain about 10–20%, toothpaste 1–2%. Irritation rises with concentration and contact time.

profile.sensitization: Irritant but not a true allergen; people with eczema or rosacea often do better without it.

myths.claim: SLS causes cancer.
myths.consensus: This traces to a 1998 chain email; SLS is not classified as a carcinogen by IARC, NTP or any regulator.

myths.claim: Sodium coco-sulfate is a gentler natural alternative.
myths.consensus: It is mostly the same molecule with a slightly broader chain-length mix, and similarly irritating.

synthesis.method: Semi-synthetic: fatty alcohol from coconut/palm kernel oil or petroleum, then sulfated.
steps: Lauryl alcohol is produced by hydrogenating coconut or palm kernel oil fatty acids.
It is sulfated with sulfur trioxide gas.
The resulting lauryl sulfuric acid is neutralized with sodium hydroxide.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Harmful to aquatic life at elevated concentrations before treatment.

fun.history: Alkyl sulfate detergents appeared in the 1930s as the first synthetic alternatives to soap that didn't form scum in hard water.
uses: SDS-PAGE, a core technique in biology labs
Whipping aid for powdered egg whites
fun.occurrence: Synthetic, though its lauryl chain comes from coconut and palm kernel oils.

name: Sodium Laureth Sulfate
scoreRationale: Milder than SLS, but ethoxylation can leave traces of 1,4-dioxane, a possible carcinogen now strictly limited in some states.
summary: SLES is the main foaming cleanser in most shampoos and body washes. It's gentler than SLS; the concern is a manufacturing contaminant, not the surfactant itself.

identity.composition: C12–C14 alkyl chains with an average of 1–3 ethylene oxide units, capped with a sodium sulfate group.

profile.function: Produces dense lather and removes oil in shampoos, body washes, hand soaps and dish detergents.

reactions.title: Ethoxylation
reactions.description: Lauryl alcohol reacts with ethylene oxide to add ether units, making the head group larger and milder.

reactions.title: 1,4-Dioxane formation
reactions.description: Two ethylene oxide units can cyclize into 1,4-dioxane, removed by vacuum stripping.

mechanisms.title: Milder barrier interaction
mechanisms.description: The ethoxylated head group forms larger micelles that penetrate the skin barrier less than SLS.

regulatory.status: Safe as used when formulated to be non-irritating.
Caps 1,4-dioxane at 1 ppm in household cleaning and personal-care products and 10 ppm in cosmetics.
1,4-Dioxane (the impurity) is Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic.

toxicology.mechanism: The surfactant itself is a mild irritant; 1,4-dioxane caused liver tumors in rodents at high doses in drinking water.
toxicology.dosage: Well-made SLES contains only trace 1,4-dioxane; wash-off exposure is brief.

profile.sensitization: Low sensitization potential; irritation depends on concentration.

myths.claim: SLES contains cancer-causing chemicals.
myths.consensus: The surfactant is not carcinogenic; the concern is a removable impurity that regulators now limit.

steps: Lauryl alcohol is ethoxylated with ethylene oxide using a base catalyst.
The ethoxylate is sulfated with sulfur trioxide.
The acid is neutralized with sodium hydroxide, then vacuum-stripped to remove 1,4-dioxane.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Toxic to aquatic life before wastewater treatment.

fun.history: Became the dominant shampoo surfactant in the 1960s–70s because it lathered well while being gentler than SLS.
fun.occurrence: Synthetic.

name: Cocamidopropyl Betaine
scoreRationale: A mild co-surfactant that reduces irritation from other cleansers, but manufacturing impurities (amidoamine, DMAPA) cause allergic reactions in some people.
summary: Cocamidopropyl betaine is a gentle, coconut-derived cleanser that softens harsher surfactants. A few people are allergic to its impurities.

identity.composition: Zwitterionic surfactants with C8–C18 coconut fatty acid chains; representative structure is lauramidopropyl betaine.

profile.function: Boosts foam and viscosity and reduces the irritation of anionic surfactants like SLES.

reactions.title: Amidation
reactions.description: Coconut fatty acids react with dimethylaminopropylamine (DMAPA) to form an amidoamine.

reactions.title: Quaternization
reactions.description: The amidoamine reacts with sodium monochloroacetate to form the betaine.

mechanisms.title: Mixed micelles
mechanisms.description: Pairs with anionic surfactants to form mixed micelles that bind less to skin proteins, lowering irritation.

mechanisms.title: Allergy from impurities
mechanisms.description: Residual amidoamine and DMAPA act as haptens that trigger allergic contact dermatitis in sensitized people.

regulatory.status: Safe when formulated to be non-sensitizing, with limits on amidoamine and DMAPA impurities.
Named Allergen of the Year in 2004.

toxicology.mechanism: Low systemic toxicity; the main hazard is contact allergy from impurities.
toxicology.dosage: Shampoos use about 1–10%.

profile.sensitization: Patch-test positivity is a few percent in dermatitis clinics; purer grades have lowered reaction rates.

myths.claim: It's natural because it comes from coconuts.
myths.consensus: The fatty chain comes from coconut oil, but it's made through chemical synthesis.

steps: Coconut oil fatty acids react with DMAPA to form cocamidopropyl dimethylamine.
The amidoamine is quaternized with sodium monochloroacetate.
The product is diluted to a roughly 30% solution.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Toxic to aquatic life at elevated concentrations.

fun.history: Adopted in the 1970s–80s as a mild surfactant for baby shampoos and "tear-free" formulas.
fun.occurrence: Synthetic, from coconut fatty acids.

name: Dimethicone
scoreRationale: Inert, non-irritating and non-sensitizing; environmental concerns apply to small cyclic siloxanes rather than dimethicone itself.
summary: Dimethicone is a silicone that makes creams feel silky, protects skin, and smooths hair. It's very well tolerated.

identity.composition: Linear polymer of repeating –Si(CH3)2–O– units capped with trimethylsilyl groups; viscosity depends on chain length.

physical.state: Clear oil ranging from water-thin to gum-like
physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; soluble in hydrocarbons

profile.function: Adds slip and a silky finish, forms a breathable protective film, reduces frizz, and prevents foaming in food frying oil.

reactions.title: Hydrolysis and polycondensation
reactions.description: Dimethyldichlorosilane reacts with water to form siloxane chains.

mechanisms.title: Skin protectant film
mechanisms.description: Forms a water-resistant but gas-permeable layer that reduces water loss and friction without blocking pores.

regulatory.status: Approved OTC skin protectant active ingredient.
Safe as used.
Restricts cyclic siloxanes D4, D5 and D6 (not dimethicone) in wash-off and leave-on products for persistence.

toxicology.mechanism: Too large to penetrate skin; biologically inert.
toxicology.dosage: Cosmetics use about 1–15%.

profile.sensitization: Among the least sensitizing cosmetic ingredients.

myths.claim: Silicones suffocate skin and clog pores.
myths.consensus: Dimethicone films are gas-permeable and tested as non-comedogenic.

myths.claim: Silicones build up and ruin hair.
myths.consensus: Heavy silicones can accumulate but wash out with regular shampoo; many are water-soluble.

synthesis.method: Synthetically manufactured from silicon and methyl chloride.
steps: Müller–Rochow direct process: silicon reacts with methyl chloride over a copper catalyst.
Dimethyldichlorosilane is hydrolyzed to siloxane oligomers.
Oligomers are polymerized to the target chain length and end-capped.

environment.persistence: Persistent in sediments but not bioaccumulative due to large size.
environment.biodegradability: Not biodegradable; degrades slowly in soil to silica and CO2.

fun.history: Frederic Kipping coined "silicone" in the early 1900s; Eugene Rochow's direct process (1940s) made silicones affordable.
uses: Anti-foaming agent in fast-food fryer oil
fun.occurrence: Synthetic.

name: Phenoxyethanol
scoreRationale: Safe at up to 1% per EU and U.S. reviews, with rare allergy; French authorities advise avoiding it in leave-on diaper-area products for toddlers.
summary: Phenoxyethanol is the most common paraben-free preservative. It's effective and well tolerated at the 1% or less used in cosmetics.

physical.state: Colorless oily liquid, faint rose odor
physical.solubility: Moderately soluble in water (about 27 g/L); soluble in oils

profile.function: Protects water-based products from bacteria, yeast and mold after opening.

reactions.title: Hydroxyethylation of phenol
reactions.description: Phenol opens the ethylene oxide ring in the presence of a base.

mechanisms.title: Membrane disruption
mechanisms.description: Increases microbial membrane permeability, causing potassium leakage and uncoupling energy production, especially in Gram-negative bacteria.

mechanisms.title: Human metabolism
mechanisms.description: Absorbed through skin and oxidized to phenoxyacetic acid, excreted in urine.

regulatory.status: Safe at up to 1% in all cosmetic products, including for children.
Recommends not using it in leave-on products for the diaper area of children under 3.
Safe at 1% or less.

toxicology.mechanism: High oral doses depress the central nervous system; an FDA 2008 warning concerned a nipple cream that infants could swallow.
toxicology.dosage: Cosmetics are capped at 1%; systemic exposure from normal use is well below levels of concern.

profile.sensitization: Contact allergy is rare, making it one of the lowest-risk preservatives.

myths.claim: Phenoxyethanol is a toxic chemical found in antifreeze.
myths.consensus: It's a glycol ether, a different compound from the ethylene glycol in antifreeze, and it's safe at cosmetic levels.

steps: Phenol reacts with ethylene oxide under basic catalysis.
The product is purified by distillation.

fun.history: Commercialized alongside the glycol-ether solvents of the early 20th century and long used as a perfume fixative before becoming a preservative.
fun.occurrence: Commercial phenoxyethanol is synthetic.

name: Methylparaben
scoreRationale: Methylparaben is considered safe at permitted levels, but parabens as a class have weak estrogenic activity and longer-chain parabens face tighter limits.
summary: Methylparaben is a long-used, low-allergy preservative. Longer-chain parabens raised hormone questions that led to limits; methylparaben is the least concerning of the group.

profile.function: Prevents mold and bacterial growth in creams, lotions and some foods.

reactions.title: Esterification
reactions.description: p-Hydroxybenzoic acid reacts with methanol to form the methyl ester.

reactions.title: Hydrolysis in the body
reactions.description: Esterases in skin and liver convert it back to p-hydroxybenzoic acid, which is excreted.

mechanisms.title: Antimicrobial action
mechanisms.description: Disrupts microbial membrane transport and mitochondrial function.

mechanisms.title: Weak estrogen receptor binding
mechanisms.description: Parabens bind estrogen receptors thousands of times more weakly than estradiol; activity increases with chain length.

regulatory.status: Methyl- and ethylparaben allowed; propyl- and butylparaben capped at 0.14% combined and banned in leave-on diaper-area products; five other parabens banned (2014).
Methylparaben is GRAS in food.
Safe at present practices of use.

toxicology.mechanism: Low acute toxicity; endocrine concerns stem from receptor binding in cell and animal studies at high doses.
toxicology.dosage: Cosmetics typically use 0.1–0.3%; urinary levels in people are far below doses that show hormonal effects in animals.

profile.sensitization: Among the least allergenic preservatives, except on damaged skin (the "paraben paradox").

myths.claim: Parabens cause breast cancer.
myths.consensus: A 2004 study detected parabens in tumor tissue but did not test healthy tissue or show causation; no causal link has been established.

steps: Kolbe–Schmitt carboxylation of potassium phenoxide yields p-hydroxybenzoic acid.
The acid is esterified with methanol using an acid catalyst.
The ester is crystallized and purified.

fun.history: Parabens have been used as preservatives since the 1920s.
fun.occurrence: Occurs naturally in blueberries and is a component of the honeybee queen's mandibular pheromone.

name: Fragrance
scoreRationale: The leading cause of cosmetic contact allergy; formulas are trade secrets, so consumers can't see which of dozens of chemicals are inside.
summary: "Fragrance" can hide dozens of scent chemicals under one word. It's the most common cause of allergic reactions to cosmetics.

identity.composition: Undisclosed blends of essential oils and synthetic aroma chemicals (for example limonene, linalool, citronellol, musks), often with solvents.

profile.function: Gives products a pleasant scent and masks the odor of other ingredients.

reactions.title: Autoxidation of terpenes
reactions.description: Common fragrance terpenes such as limonene and linalool react with air to form hydroperoxides, which are much stronger allergens than the fresh molecules.

mechanisms.title: Allergic contact dermatitis
mechanisms.description: Small reactive molecules (haptens) bind skin proteins, and the immune system learns to attack them (type IV hypersensitivity).

regulatory.status: 26 fragrance allergens must be named on labels above 0.001% in leave-on or 0.01% in rinse-off products; a 2023 update expands this to about 80 allergens.
Requires FDA to issue a rule for fragrance allergen labeling.
Industry standards restrict or ban specific fragrance materials.

toxicology.mechanism: Sensitization and irritation; some solvents historically used (like diethyl phthalate) have raised separate questions.
toxicology.dosage: Perfumes contain 10–30% fragrance; lotions and cleaners usually under 1%.

profile.sensitization: Fragrance allergy affects roughly 1–4% of the general population and is a top cause of cosmetic dermatitis.

myths.claim: "Unscented" means fragrance-free.
myths.consensus: Unscented products may contain masking fragrance; "fragrance-free" is the better choice for allergies.

myths.claim: Natural essential oils are safer than synthetic fragrance.
myths.consensus: Essential oils contain the same allergens, such as limonene and linalool, and are common causes of dermatitis.

synthesis.method: Blended from natural extracts and synthetic aroma chemicals.
steps: Perfumers combine top, middle and base notes from dozens of ingredients.
Components are dissolved in ethanol or carrier solvents.
The blend is aged and added at low levels to products.

environment.persistence: Varies; some synthetic musks are persistent.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Some components (like musks) are toxic to aquatic life.

fun.history: Chanel No. 5 (1921) was among the first perfumes to rely on synthetic aldehydes, launching modern perfumery.
fun.occurrence: Components come from flowers, woods, citrus peels and petrochemicals.

name: Hyaluronic Acid
scoreRationale: A molecule the body makes itself; extremely well tolerated with a strong hydration record.
summary: Hyaluronic acid is a natural skin molecule that binds water and plumps the skin's surface. It's one of the gentlest actives available.

identity.composition: Linear polysaccharide of repeating D-glucuronic acid and N-acetyl-D-glucosamine units; cosmetic grades range from about 5 kDa to 2,000 kDa.

profile.function: Hydrates and plumps the skin's surface, improves texture, and gives serums a smooth glide.

reactions.title: Water binding
reactions.description: Its many carboxylate and hydroxyl groups hydrogen-bond with water, forming a hydrated gel network.

reactions.title: Enzymatic breakdown
reactions.description: Hyaluronidase enzymes cut it into smaller fragments; the body turns over about a third of its HA daily.

mechanisms.title: Surface film vs. penetration
mechanisms.description: High-molecular-weight HA stays on the surface as a hydrating film; low-molecular-weight fragments penetrate the upper skin layers.

mechanisms.title: CD44 signaling
mechanisms.description: HA interacts with the CD44 receptor, which influences wound healing and cell migration.

regulatory.status: Safe as used.
Regulated as a device in dermal fillers and joint injections.

toxicology.mechanism: Non-toxic; it's a natural component of skin, joints and eyes.
toxicology.dosage: Serums typically contain 0.1–2%.

profile.sensitization: Essentially non-sensitizing.

myths.claim: Hyaluronic acid holds 1,000 times its weight in water.
myths.consensus: It binds a lot of water, but this marketing number doesn't reflect what happens on skin.

myths.claim: HA dries out skin in dry climates.
myths.consensus: It works best with an occlusive moisturizer on top, but it doesn't dehydrate skin.

synthesis.method: Bio-fermented by Streptococcus zooepidemicus or engineered Bacillus.
steps: Bacteria ferment glucose and secrete hyaluronic acid.
It is purified by filtration and alcohol precipitation.
It may be hydrolyzed to lower molecular weights.

fun.history: Karl Meyer and John Palmer isolated it from cow eyes in 1934, naming it from Greek "hyalos" (glass) plus uronic acid. It was once harvested from rooster combs.
fun.occurrence: Skin, joint fluid, the vitreous humor of the eye and umbilical cords.

name: Niacinamide
scoreRationale: A vitamin with strong evidence for barrier and pigmentation benefits and a wide safety margin; high percentages can cause mild flushing.
summary: Niacinamide is a form of vitamin B3 that strengthens the skin barrier, evens tone and calms redness. It's gentle and well researched.

profile.function: Improves barrier function, reduces hyperpigmentation and redness, and fortifies foods as vitamin B3.

reactions.title: NAD+ biosynthesis
reactions.description: Converted in cells into NAD+ and NADP+, coenzymes for hundreds of redox reactions.

reactions.title: Hydrolysis to niacin
reactions.description: Heat and strong acid or base can slowly hydrolyze it to nicotinic acid, which causes flushing.

mechanisms.title: Barrier repair
mechanisms.description: Increases ceramide and free fatty acid synthesis in the stratum corneum, reducing water loss.

mechanisms.title: Pigment transfer inhibition
mechanisms.description: Reduces transfer of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes, fading dark spots.

mechanisms.title: DNA repair support
mechanisms.description: Oral nicotinamide (500 mg twice daily) reduced new non-melanoma skin cancers by 23% in high-risk patients in the ONTRAC trial (2015).

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe as a nutrient.
Safe as used.

toxicology.mechanism: Very high oral doses (grams per day) can stress the liver; topical use is low risk.
toxicology.dosage: Serums typically use 2–10%; benefits are seen at 2–5%.

profile.sensitization: Rarely sensitizing; high concentrations can cause temporary redness or tingling.

myths.claim: Never combine niacinamide with vitamin C.
myths.consensus: Conversion to flushing niacin requires high heat over time; modern formulas can be combined safely.

steps: 3-Methylpyridine undergoes ammoxidation to 3-cyanopyridine.
The enzyme nitrile hydratase (from Rhodococcus rhodochrous) converts the nitrile to niacinamide.
The product is crystallized.

fun.history: Conrad Elvehjem identified nicotinic acid and its amide as cures for canine black tongue in 1937, solving pellagra, which had killed thousands in the American South.
fun.occurrence: Meat, fish, mushrooms and yeast; the body also makes it from tryptophan.

name: Salicylic Acid
scoreRationale: An effective, FDA-recognized acne active, but it can irritate, and large-area use is not advised for young children or in pregnancy at high strength.
summary: Salicylic acid is an oil-soluble exfoliant that clears pores and treats acne. Effective at 0.5–2%, but it can dry or irritate skin.

physical.solubility: Slightly soluble in water (about 2 g/L); soluble in ethanol and oils

profile.function: Exfoliates inside pores, reduces acne lesions and treats dandruff, warts and calluses.

reactions.title: Kolbe–Schmitt carboxylation
reactions.description: Sodium phenoxide reacts with CO2 under heat and pressure, then acid releases salicylic acid.

reactions.title: Acetylation to aspirin
reactions.description: Reacting with acetic anhydride produces acetylsalicylic acid.

mechanisms.title: Comedolysis
mechanisms.description: Being lipid-soluble, it penetrates sebum-filled pores and loosens connections between corneocytes.

mechanisms.title: Anti-inflammatory action
mechanisms.description: Modulates inflammatory signaling (related to aspirin's effects), calming red acne lesions.

regulatory.status: OTC acne drug monograph.
Allowed as a preservative and for other uses; not for children under 3 except in shampoos.
regulatory.limit: Up to 2% (3% in rinse-off hair products)

toxicology.mechanism: Absorbed salicylate can cause salicylism (ringing ears, nausea) when used over large areas, especially in children.
toxicology.dosage: Face products use 0.5–2%; wart removers up to 40% on small areas.

profile.sensitization: Allergy is uncommon; people with aspirin allergy should be cautious.

myths.claim: Willow bark extract works the same as salicylic acid.
myths.consensus: Willow bark contains salicin and very little free salicylic acid, so it's much weaker.

synthesis.method: Synthetically manufactured via the Kolbe–Schmitt reaction.
steps: Phenol is converted to sodium phenoxide with sodium hydroxide.
It is heated with CO2 at about 125 °C and 100 atm.
Sulfuric acid converts sodium salicylate to salicylic acid, which is recrystallized.

fun.history: Willow bark remedies go back to ancient Sumer and Egypt; Raffaele Piria made salicylic acid in 1838, and Bayer's Felix Hoffmann made aspirin from it in 1897.
fun.occurrence: Plants use it as a hormone to signal defense against pathogens; found in willow and wintergreen as related compounds.

name: Retinol
scoreRationale: One of the best-proven anti-aging actives, but it commonly irritates, increases sun sensitivity, and is advised against in pregnancy; the EU capped concentrations in 2024.
summary: Retinol is a vitamin A derivative that speeds skin renewal and builds collagen. It works, but start slowly, use sunscreen and skip it in pregnancy.

physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; soluble in oils
physical.phStability: Unstable to light, air and heat; needs protective packaging

profile.function: Reduces fine lines, evens texture and pigmentation, and treats acne.

reactions.title: Stepwise oxidation
reactions.description: Skin enzymes convert retinol to retinaldehyde and then retinoic acid, the active form.

reactions.title: Photodegradation
reactions.description: UV light breaks its conjugated double bonds, which is why it's used at night in opaque packaging.

mechanisms.title: Nuclear receptor signaling
mechanisms.description: Retinoic acid binds RAR/RXR receptors, switching on genes that increase cell turnover and collagen production and reduce collagen-degrading MMP enzymes.

regulatory.status: Caps vitamin A in cosmetics.
regulatory.limit: 0.05% retinol equivalent in body lotions; 0.3% in face and hand products

regulatory.status: Cosmetic ingredient; prescription retinoids (tretinoin) are drugs.

toxicology.mechanism: High systemic vitamin A is teratogenic; topical cosmetic retinol is minimally absorbed, but avoidance in pregnancy is standard advice.
toxicology.dosage: Cosmetics typically 0.01–1%. Irritation ("retinization") usually subsides after a few weeks.

profile.sensitization: Irritation is common; true allergy is rare.

myths.claim: Retinol thins your skin.
myths.consensus: It thins the outermost dead layer slightly but thickens the living epidermis and increases collagen over time.

myths.claim: You can't use retinol in summer.
myths.consensus: You can, with daily sunscreen; it increases sensitivity to sunburn.

steps: β-Ionone is built into a C15 or C20 intermediate (Roche Isler or BASF Wittig routes).
Coupling steps assemble the full polyene chain.
The product is stabilized, often as retinyl acetate or palmitate.

fun.history: Vitamin A was discovered in 1913; Paul Karrer determined retinol's structure in 1931, and Otto Isler achieved industrial synthesis in 1947.
uses: Treating vitamin A deficiency, a leading cause of childhood blindness
fun.occurrence: Liver, eggs and dairy; plants provide beta-carotene, which the body converts to retinol.

name: Zinc Oxide
scoreRationale: One of only two sunscreen filters the FDA proposes as generally safe and effective; gentle on sensitive skin. Avoid inhaling sprays and powders.
summary: Zinc oxide is a mineral sunscreen that blocks UVA and UVB and soothes diaper rash. It's very gentle on skin.

physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; dissolves in acids
physical.phStability: Amphoteric; dissolves in strong acids and bases

profile.function: Provides broad-spectrum UV protection, protects and soothes irritated skin, and adds opacity.

reactions.title: UV absorption
reactions.description: As a semiconductor with a 3.37 eV band gap, ZnO absorbs UVB and UVA up to about 380 nm.

reactions.title: Amphoteric behavior
reactions.description: Dissolves in acids and bases.

mechanisms.title: Skin protectant
mechanisms.description: Forms a physical barrier and releases small amounts of zinc ions with mild antimicrobial and healing effects.

regulatory.status: Generally recognized as safe and effective sunscreen active.
Safe as a UV filter, including nano forms, except in sprayable products that may be inhaled.

toxicology.mechanism: Does not penetrate intact skin; inhaled zinc oxide fumes (metalworking) cause "metal fume fever".
toxicology.dosage: Sunscreens use 5–25%; diaper creams 10–40%.

profile.sensitization: Non-sensitizing; ideal for sensitive and infant skin.

myths.claim: Nano zinc oxide enters the bloodstream.
myths.consensus: Studies show nanoparticles remain on the outer skin layers.

synthesis.method: Synthetically manufactured from zinc metal or ore.
steps: French process: zinc metal is vaporized and oxidized in air.
Particles are collected, classified by size, and sometimes coated.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Zinc ions are toxic to some aquatic organisms at elevated concentrations.

fun.history: Zinc oxide ointments appear in ancient Indian and Greek medicine; alchemists called it "philosopher's wool".
fun.occurrence: The mineral zincite.

name: Methylisothiazolinone
scoreRationale: A potent skin sensitizer that caused an allergy epidemic in the 2010s; banned from leave-on cosmetics in the EU and tightly limited elsewhere.
summary: MIT is a strong preservative in cleaners and some rinse-off products. It is one of the most common causes of contact allergy.

profile.function: Kills bacteria and fungi in water-based products at parts-per-million levels.

reactions.title: Thiol attack
reactions.description: Its electrophilic N–S bond reacts with cysteine thiols in proteins, opening the ring and forming mixed disulfides.

mechanisms.title: Enzyme inhibition
mechanisms.description: Inactivates microbial dehydrogenase enzymes that rely on thiol groups, halting respiration.

mechanisms.title: Haptenation of skin proteins
mechanisms.description: The same reactivity lets it bind skin proteins, making it a strong sensitizer.

regulatory.status: Banned in leave-on cosmetics since 2017.
Mixtures with 15 ppm or more must warn that they may produce an allergic reaction.
Allergen of the Year 2013.

toxicology.mechanism: Sensitization via haptenation; also toxic to aquatic organisms.
toxicology.dosage: Cleaners and paints often contain tens of ppm; once sensitized, reactions can occur at a few ppm, including from paint fumes.

profile.sensitization: Strong sensitizer; sensitization rates in European patch-test clinics exceeded 5% at the epidemic's peak.

myths.claim: Rinse-off products with MIT are completely safe.
myths.consensus: Rinse-off exposure is lower, but people already sensitized can still react.

steps: N-Methyl-3-mercaptopropionamide (or its disulfide) is cyclized with a chlorinating agent.
This produces a mixture of MCI and MI, which can be separated.

fun.history: The MCI/MI blend (Kathon CG) was introduced around 1980; when MI alone was allowed at higher levels in the 2000s, allergy rates surged.
fun.occurrence: Synthetic.

name: Cetearyl Alcohol
scoreRationale: A gentle fatty alcohol, not a drying alcohol; rare contact allergy is the only notable caution.
summary: Cetearyl alcohol is a waxy fatty alcohol that thickens creams and softens skin. Despite the name, it isn't drying like rubbing alcohol.

identity.composition: Mixture of cetyl alcohol (C16) and stearyl alcohol (C18).

physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; soluble in oils

profile.function: Thickens and stabilizes emulsions and conditions skin and hair.

reactions.title: Fatty acid hydrogenation
reactions.description: Methyl esters of plant fatty acids are hydrogenated to fatty alcohols.

mechanisms.title: Lamellar gel networks
mechanisms.description: With emulsifiers it forms layered gel structures that trap water and give creams body.

regulatory.status: Safe as used.
Permitted as an indirect and direct food additive in specific uses.

toxicology.mechanism: Very low toxicity; not absorbed meaningfully.
toxicology.dosage: Creams use about 1–5%.

profile.sensitization: Rare contact allergy, sometimes from impurities.

myths.claim: All alcohols in skincare dry out skin.
myths.consensus: Fatty alcohols are waxy emollients unrelated to ethanol's solvent action.

synthesis.method: Semi-synthetic, from coconut or palm oil fatty acids.
steps: Fatty acids or methyl esters are hydrogenated over a copper catalyst.
C16 and C18 fractions are blended.

fun.history: Michel Eugène Chevreul isolated cetyl alcohol from spermaceti (sperm whale oil) in 1817; "cetyl" comes from Latin cetus, whale.
fun.occurrence: Plant waxes and, historically, whale oil.

name: Propylene Glycol
scoreRationale: Low toxicity with decades of use, but it can irritate or sensitize some people and was the 2018 Allergen of the Year.
summary: Propylene glycol keeps products moist and dissolves other ingredients. It's low in toxicity but can irritate sensitive skin.

physical.solubility: Miscible with water, ethanol and acetone

profile.function: Retains moisture, dissolves flavors and actives, enhances penetration, and lowers the freezing point.

reactions.title: Hydration of propylene oxide
reactions.description: Industrial production opens the epoxide ring with water.

reactions.title: Metabolism
reactions.description: Alcohol dehydrogenase converts it to lactic acid, a normal metabolite.

mechanisms.title: Penetration enhancement
mechanisms.description: Temporarily loosens stratum corneum lipids, helping other ingredients penetrate (which can also increase irritation).

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
ADI 25 mg/kg body weight; EU food use limited to carrier roles.
Allergen of the Year 2018.

toxicology.mechanism: Very high intravenous doses in hospital drug formulations can cause lactic acidosis.
toxicology.dosage: Cosmetics use 1–20%; foods use small amounts as a carrier.

profile.sensitization: Irritant reactions are more common than true allergy, especially at high concentrations.

myths.claim: Propylene glycol is antifreeze.
myths.consensus: Toxic antifreeze is ethylene glycol; propylene glycol is used in "pet-safe" antifreeze because it's far less toxic.

synthesis.method: Synthetically manufactured from propylene; bio-based versions are made from glycerin.
steps: Propylene is oxidized to propylene oxide.
Propylene oxide is hydrated with water.
The glycol is distilled to USP grade.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Low, though large de-icing runoff can deplete oxygen in streams.

fun.history: Charles-Adolphe Wurtz first prepared it in 1859.
fun.occurrence: Synthetic, though microbes produce it in some fermentations.

name: Panthenol
scoreRationale: A provitamin with excellent tolerance and evidence for barrier repair and soothing.
summary: Panthenol (provitamin B5) hydrates, soothes and helps skin and hair repair. It's gentle enough for babies.

physical.state: Clear viscous liquid (D-form) or white powder (DL-form)
physical.solubility: Freely soluble in water and alcohol

profile.function: Moisturizes, calms irritation, supports healing, and adds shine to hair.

reactions.title: Enzymatic oxidation
reactions.description: In skin, panthenol is oxidized to pantothenic acid (vitamin B5).

mechanisms.title: Coenzyme A synthesis
mechanisms.description: Pantothenic acid is a building block of coenzyme A, needed for lipid synthesis in barrier repair.

mechanisms.title: Fibroblast activation
mechanisms.description: Studies show it promotes fibroblast proliferation and wound re-epithelialization.

regulatory.status: Safe as used.
Dexpanthenol ointments are widely approved for minor wounds and diaper rash.

toxicology.mechanism: Essentially non-toxic.
toxicology.dosage: Cosmetics use 0.5–5%.

profile.sensitization: Rare contact allergy.

myths.claim: Panthenol makes hair grow thicker.
myths.consensus: It coats and hydrates hair, making it look fuller, but it doesn't increase hair growth.

steps: D-pantolactone is prepared and resolved.
It is condensed with 3-aminopropanol to form D-panthenol.

fun.history: Roger J. Williams discovered pantothenic acid in 1933, naming it from Greek "pantothen", meaning "from everywhere".
fun.occurrence: Pantothenic acid is found in nearly all foods.

name: Aloe Vera
scoreRationale: Decolorized inner-leaf gel is gentle and soothing; whole-leaf extracts containing aloin carry a possible-carcinogen classification.
summary: Aloe vera gel soothes and hydrates skin. The purified inner gel used in cosmetics is gentle; unpurified whole-leaf extracts are a different story.

identity.composition: About 99% water, with polysaccharides (acemannan), glycoproteins, vitamins and minerals.

physical.phStability: Oxidizes and loses activity over time

profile.function: Soothes, hydrates, and provides a cooling feel in after-sun and sensitive-skin products.

reactions.title: Polysaccharide film
reactions.description: Acemannan forms a hydrating, film-forming layer on skin.

mechanisms.title: Anti-inflammatory activity
mechanisms.description: Compounds in aloe gel may reduce inflammatory mediators and support wound healing; clinical evidence is mixed.

regulatory.status: Whole-leaf aloe extract (non-decolorized) is Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic, based on a rat drinking-water study.
Removed aloe as an approved OTC laxative ingredient.
Safe in cosmetics when anthraquinone (aloin) levels are limited.

toxicology.mechanism: Aloin and other anthraquinones in the leaf's outer layer are laxatives and caused intestinal tumors in rats.
toxicology.dosage: Cosmetic grades are decolorized with aloin typically below 50 ppm.

profile.sensitization: Rare allergy, more common in people allergic to lily-family plants.

myths.claim: Aloe heals burns completely.
myths.consensus: It can soothe minor sunburn, but evidence for faster healing is mixed, and it shouldn't be used on serious burns.

steps: Leaves are harvested and the outer rind (containing aloin) is removed.
The inner gel is filleted, homogenized and filtered.
Activated charcoal decolorization removes remaining anthraquinones.

fun.history: Aloe appears in the Egyptian Ebers Papyrus (about 1550 BCE) as a remedy.
fun.occurrence: Aloe barbadensis Miller, native to the Arabian Peninsula.

name: Shea Butter
scoreRationale: A gentle plant fat with a long history of use; refined shea contains almost no nut protein.
summary: Shea butter is a rich plant fat that softens and protects dry skin. It's gentle and supports women's cooperatives in West Africa.

identity.composition: Triglycerides of stearic and oleic acids plus 5–10% unsaponifiables (triterpene esters, phytosterols, vitamin E).

profile.function: Softens and occludes dry skin, adds richness to balms and creams, and conditions hair.

reactions.title: Saponification
reactions.description: Like other fats, it reacts with lye to form soap and glycerin.

mechanisms.title: Occlusion and lipid replenishment
mechanisms.description: Forms a protective film that reduces water loss; its triterpene esters have anti-inflammatory activity in lab studies.

regulatory.status: Safe as used.
Shea is one of six vegetable fats allowed in chocolate up to 5%.

toxicology.mechanism: Non-toxic.
toxicology.dosage: Balms can be up to 100% shea.

profile.sensitization: Botanically a tree nut, but refined shea contains negligible protein; allergic reactions are very rare.

myths.claim: Shea butter clogs pores.
myths.consensus: It rates low on comedogenicity scales, though very heavy use can feel greasy on oily skin.

steps: Nuts are dried, cracked, roasted and ground.
The paste is kneaded with water to separate the fat.
The butter is boiled, filtered and optionally refined and deodorized.

environment.notes: Shea trees grow wild and are not plantation-farmed; the trade provides income for millions of women in the Sahel.

fun.history: Used for centuries across the Sahel for cooking, medicine and skincare; sometimes called "women's gold".
fun.occurrence: Nuts of the shea tree (Vitellaria paradoxa).

name: Disodium EDTA
scoreRationale: Safe at cosmetic and food levels, but poorly biodegradable, persisting in waterways and mobilizing heavy metals.
summary: EDTA traps metal ions so products stay stable and preservatives work better. Safe for people, but it lingers in the environment.

physical.phStability: Stable; binding strength depends on pH

profile.function: Binds calcium, magnesium and trace metals to prevent rancidity, color changes and scum, and boosts preservatives and cleaners.

reactions.title: Chelation
reactions.description: EDTA wraps around metal ions with six binding sites, forming very stable complexes.

mechanisms.title: Preservative boosting
mechanisms.description: Removing metal ions destabilizes bacterial outer membranes, making preservatives more effective.

regulatory.status: Safe as used.
Calcium disodium EDTA permitted in foods with limits.
ADI 0–2.5 mg/kg body weight (as calcium disodium EDTA).

toxicology.mechanism: Poorly absorbed through skin or gut; intravenous doses can deplete calcium.
toxicology.dosage: Cosmetics use 0.05–0.2%.

profile.sensitization: Rare.

myths.claim: EDTA is a penetration enhancer that drags toxins into your body.
myths.consensus: At cosmetic levels it has minimal effect on skin penetration.

steps: Ethylenediamine reacts with formaldehyde and sodium cyanide.
The tetrasodium salt is partially acidified to disodium EDTA and crystallized.
equations: H2NCH2CH2NH2 + 4 CH2O + 4 NaCN + 4 H2O → Na4EDTA + 4 NH3

environment.persistence: Persistent; one of the most abundant synthetic chemicals in European surface waters.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Low direct toxicity, but it can remobilize heavy metals from sediments.

fun.history: Ferdinand Münz developed EDTA at IG Farben in 1935 as a citric acid substitute for textile dyeing.
fun.occurrence: Synthetic only.

name: Sodium Hypochlorite
scoreRationale: A highly effective disinfectant, but corrosive to skin, eyes and lungs, and dangerous when mixed with acids or ammonia.
summary: Bleach kills germs and whitens by oxidation. Use it diluted, ventilated, and never mix it with ammonia or acidic cleaners.

physical.state: Pale greenish-yellow liquid (3–8% in household bleach)
physical.phStability: Alkaline (pH 11–13); decomposes with heat, light and acid

profile.function: Disinfects surfaces and water, removes stains and mildew, and whitens laundry.

reactions.title: Hypochlorous acid equilibrium
reactions.description: In water, hypochlorite forms hypochlorous acid (HOCl), the more potent germ killer; the balance depends on pH (pKa about 7.5).

reactions.title: Chlorine gas with acids
reactions.description: Mixing with acidic toilet cleaners or vinegar releases toxic chlorine gas.

reactions.title: Chloramines with ammonia
reactions.description: Mixing with ammonia-based glass cleaners forms toxic chloramine vapors.

mechanisms.title: Oxidative killing
mechanisms.description: HOCl oxidizes thiol groups, chlorinates amines, and unfolds proteins and DNA in microbes within seconds.

mechanisms.title: Innate immunity parallel
mechanisms.description: Human neutrophils make the same HOCl with the enzyme myeloperoxidase to kill bacteria.

regulatory.status: Registered disinfectant under FIFRA when making germ-kill claims.

Labels must warn: "Do not use together with other products. May release dangerous gases (chlorine)."

toxicology.mechanism: Oxidizes and saponifies tissue; inhaled chlorine or chloramine gas forms acids in the airways causing inflammation and fluid in the lungs.
toxicology.dosage: Household bleach is 3–8%; recommended disinfecting dilutions are about 0.1–0.5%. Swallowing small amounts usually causes only irritation; mixing gases send thousands to U.S. poison centers every year.

profile.sensitization: Irritant rather than allergen; repeated cleaning exposure is associated with asthma in cleaning workers.

myths.claim: More bleach cleans better.
myths.consensus: Bleach disinfects and whitens but doesn't remove dirt; clean first, then disinfect at the labeled dilution.

myths.claim: Bleach is "toxic waste" that persists in the environment.
myths.consensus: It breaks down quickly to salt and water, though it can form chlorinated by-products with organic matter.

synthesis.method: Synthetically manufactured from chlorine and sodium hydroxide.
steps: Brine is electrolyzed to produce chlorine and sodium hydroxide (chlor-alkali process).
Chlorine gas is bubbled into cold sodium hydroxide solution.
The solution is diluted and stabilized with a little extra lye.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Very toxic to aquatic life in concentrated form; can form trihalomethanes and other by-products.

fun.history: Claude Louis Berthollet invented the first chlorine bleach, "Eau de Javel," near Paris in 1789; Henry Dakin's dilute hypochlorite solution saved countless wounded soldiers in World War I.
fun.occurrence: Made naturally by white blood cells to destroy pathogens.

scoreRationale: An excellent solvent and disinfectant, but flammable, drying at high skincare concentrations, and toxic when swallowed by children.

physical.solubility: Miscible with water and most solvents

profile.function: Dissolves fragrances and actives, preserves, gives a quick-drying feel, and disinfects hands and surfaces.

reactions.title: Fermentation

reactions.title: Metabolic oxidation

mechanisms.title: Protein denaturation

mechanisms.title: Skin lipid extraction

regulatory.status: Hand sanitizers must contain 60–95% ethanol.

toxicology.mechanism: Central nervous system depressant when ingested; acetaldehyde is the carcinogenic metabolite.
toxicology.dosage: Swallowing hand sanitizer can cause alcohol poisoning in young children; topical use is low risk.

profile.sensitization: Rarely allergenic; can sting broken skin.

myths.claim: Any alcohol in skincare ruins your skin barrier.
myths.consensus: High levels can be drying with frequent use, but low levels in well-formulated products have modest effects.

synthesis.method: Bio-fermented from sugars and starches, or synthesized from ethylene.
steps: Yeast ferment sugar cane, corn or grain mash.
The beer is distilled to 95% ethanol.

environment.notes: A volatile organic compound that contributes to smog formation.

fun.history: Distillation of alcohol was refined by Arab alchemists such as al-Kindi in the 9th century; the word "alcohol" comes from Arabic al-kuḥl.
fun.occurrence: Ripe fruit, fermented sap, and even vast interstellar clouds like Sagittarius B2.

reactions.title: Oxidation to acetone

myths.claim: Higher-percentage alcohol always disinfects better.

steps: Propene is hydrated indirectly with sulfuric acid or directly over acid catalysts.

fun.history: The first commercial petrochemical, produced by Standard Oil of New Jersey in 1920.

scoreRationale: Corrosive, irritating to airways, and forms toxic gases when mixed with bleach.
summary: Ammonia cuts grease and leaves glass streak-free. Its fumes irritate lungs, and it must never be mixed with bleach.

physical.solubility: Ammonia is highly soluble in water

profile.function: Removes grease and evaporates without residue in glass cleaners; opens hair cuticles in permanent hair dyes.

reactions.title: Chloramine formation

mechanisms.title: Airway irritation

toxicology.mechanism: Alkaline burns and airway inflammation; very high inhaled concentrations can cause fluid in the lungs.
toxicology.dosage: Household ammonia is 5–10%; the smell is noticeable at around 5 ppm, well below harmful levels.

myths.claim: Mixing ammonia and bleach makes a stronger cleaner.

fun.occurrence: Produced by decomposition of urea and proteins; found in the atmospheres of Jupiter and Saturn.

name: Sodium Dodecylbenzenesulfonate
scoreRationale: The world's most-used detergent surfactant: readily biodegradable, but a skin and eye irritant and harmful to aquatic life before treatment.
summary: LAS is the main cleaning agent in most laundry detergents. It biodegrades well but irritates skin and eyes.

physical.state: White to yellow powder or paste
physical.phStability: Stable across pH; tolerant of hard water with builders

profile.function: Lifts and suspends oily soils in laundry and dish detergents.

reactions.title: Sulfonation
reactions.description: Linear alkylbenzene is sulfonated with sulfur trioxide, then neutralized.

reactions.title: Neutralization
reactions.description: The sulfonic acid is neutralized with sodium hydroxide.

mechanisms.title: Detergency
mechanisms.description: Adsorbs at fabric and oil surfaces, lowering interfacial tension so oils roll up and wash away in micelles.

regulatory.status: Surfactants must meet ready-biodegradability criteria, which LAS does.
Warning: harmful if swallowed, causes skin irritation and serious eye damage; harmful to aquatic life.

toxicology.mechanism: Membrane and protein disruption causes irritation; not genotoxic or carcinogenic.
toxicology.dosage: Laundry detergents contain about 5–25%.

profile.sensitization: Irritant, not a sensitizer.

myths.claim: Detergent foam in rivers means detergents don't biodegrade.
myths.consensus: That was true of branched ABS in the 1950s; linear LAS replaced it and degrades within days.

steps: Benzene is alkylated with linear C10–C14 olefins to form linear alkylbenzene.
It is sulfonated with SO3 and neutralized with sodium hydroxide.

environment.biodegradability: Readily biodegradable (aerobic); persists longer in anaerobic sediments.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Harmful to aquatic life before wastewater treatment.

fun.history: In the early 1960s, branched detergent surfactants caused foam on rivers and even in tap water; the U.S. industry switched to linear LAS in 1965.
fun.occurrence: Synthetic.

name: Limonene
scoreRationale: A natural citrus solvent, but it oxidizes into skin sensitizers and reacts with indoor ozone to form formaldehyde and fine particles.
summary: Limonene gives cleaners and cosmetics a citrus scent and dissolves grease. Natural, but aged limonene is a common skin allergen.

physical.state: Colorless oily liquid with orange scent
physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; miscible with oils and alcohol

profile.function: Dissolves grease, adhesives and tar, and adds a fresh citrus scent.

reactions.title: Autoxidation
reactions.description: On exposure to air, limonene forms hydroperoxides, carvone and limonene oxide; the hydroperoxides are potent skin sensitizers.

reactions.title: Indoor ozone chemistry
reactions.description: Reacts with ozone indoors to form formaldehyde and secondary organic aerosol particles.

mechanisms.title: Allergic contact dermatitis
mechanisms.description: Oxidized limonene haptens bind skin proteins and trigger T-cell-mediated allergy.

regulatory.status: Must be named on labels above 0.001% (leave-on) or 0.01% (rinse-off) as a fragrance allergen.
Generally Recognized as Safe as a flavoring.
Warning: flammable, skin irritant and sensitizer, very toxic to aquatic life.

toxicology.mechanism: Sensitization and irritation; aspiration hazard if swallowed.
toxicology.dosage: Cleaners may contain 1–20%; cosmetics usually under 1%.

profile.sensitization: Oxidized limonene is among the most frequent fragrance allergens in patch testing.

myths.claim: Natural citrus cleaners are completely non-toxic.
myths.consensus: Limonene is natural but still a sensitizer and an aquatic toxin.

steps: Orange peels from juice production are cold-pressed or steam-distilled.
The oil (over 90% limonene) is distilled to purify it.

environment.notes: A volatile organic compound that contributes to indoor air pollution chemistry.

fun.history: Named after the lemon; commercial d-limonene is a by-product of the orange juice industry.
fun.occurrence: Makes up over 90% of orange peel oil.

name: Protease
scoreRationale: Lets detergents clean at lower temperatures, but enzyme dust is a respiratory sensitizer, so products use encapsulated granules.
summary: Protease enzymes break down protein stains like blood, egg and grass. They're safe in finished detergents but can cause allergies as dust.

identity.composition: Serine protease enzymes (subtilisins) produced by Bacillus bacteria, supplied as encapsulated granules or stabilized liquids.

profile.function: Digests protein stains into small, water-soluble peptides, enabling cold-water washing.

reactions.title: Peptide-bond hydrolysis
reactions.description: The enzyme adds water across peptide bonds in protein stains.

mechanisms.title: Catalytic triad
mechanisms.description: A serine–histidine–aspartate triad in the active site attacks the peptide bond.

mechanisms.title: Respiratory sensitization
mechanisms.description: Inhaled enzyme protein can trigger IgE-mediated allergy and asthma.

regulatory.status: Danger: may cause allergy or asthma symptoms if inhaled (H334).
Manufacturers monitor workplace enzyme exposure and encapsulate enzymes to prevent dust.

toxicology.mechanism: Low toxicity except as an airborne allergen.
toxicology.dosage: Detergents contain well under 1% active enzyme protein.

profile.sensitization: Respiratory sensitizer as dust; skin contact with finished detergents rarely causes problems.

myths.claim: Enzyme detergents eat your skin.
myths.consensus: They are designed for stains; consumer skin reactions are uncommon at use concentrations.

steps: Engineered Bacillus strains secrete protease in large fermenters.
The enzyme is recovered, concentrated and encapsulated or stabilized.
Protein engineering improves stability against bleach and heat.

fun.history: Otto Röhm made the first enzyme detergent, Burnus, in 1913 using pancreatic enzymes; bacterial proteases took over in the 1960s.
fun.occurrence: Soil bacteria like Bacillus subtilis.
